title: PUBLIC NOTICE15th Jul 2026
text: The Commission reminds all voters that taking photographs or recording images of marked ballot papers inside the polling booth is strictly prohibited and constitutes an election offence under Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act, No. 37 of 2016. Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act states that a person attending any proceedings relating to an election who, without lawful excuse, captures an image of any marked ballot for purposes of financial gain or for showing allegiance, commits an offence. The offence is punishable by a fine not exceeding KSh 1 million, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The Commission urges all voters to comply with this legal requirement in order to protect the secrecy and integrity of the ballot. For accurate and up-to-date information, please visit our official website (https://iebc.or.ke) and follow our verified social media platforms (@IEBCKenya). #16thJulyByElection #YourVoteYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC, HURIA Explore Partnership to Strengthen Voter Education and Youth Civic Participation14th Jul 2026
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), today led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdalla, OGW, held a meeting with Human Rights Agenda (HURIA), a human rights organization based in Kenya's Coast region. The purpose of the meeting was to explore areas of collaboration that complement the Commission's constitutional mandate. Speaking during the meeting, the Vice Chairperson thanked the HURIA team for seeking to partner with the Commission in ensuring that young people are actively involved in educating their peers on issues that matter to them, particularly civic participation, inclusion and voter registration. She reaffirmed the Commission's commitment to strengthening collaboration with HURIA to enhance voter education initiatives at the grassroots, ensuring that young people and all eligible Kenyans receive accurate and timely information to enable them to make informed electoral decisions. She emphasized that voting is a constitutional right of every Kenyan and that providing voter education remains a core mandate of the IEBC. HURIA is currently preparing to implement a five-year programme, Rebuilding the Youth–State Social Contract as a Foundation for Enduring Security, Stability and Democratic Resilience at the Coast , which seeks to strengthen trust between young people and public institutions. The programme adopts a human rights-based approach to strengthening democratic resilience by addressing the underlying drivers of mistrust, exclusion, insecurity and violence affecting young people. #16thJulyByElection #YourVoteYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC Electoral Code Committee Finds Nakuru Town East MP Guilty of Code of Conduct Breach14th Jul 2026
text: The IEBC Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee, chaired by Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, has found the Member of the National Assembly for Nakuru Town East, Hon. title: Press Release -  Update on Preparedness for the 16th July 2026 Ol Kalou By-Election14th Jul 2026
text: The Commission wishes to inform the nation that all preparations for the by-election scheduled for Thursday, 16th July 2026, to fill the position of Member of National Assembly for Ol Kalou Constituency in Nyandarua County are progressing as planned. All registered voters in Ol Kalou Constituency MUST present their national identity card or valid passport on polling day, as these remain the primary identification documents required for voting. The Register of Voters for the Ol Kalou Constituency by-election remains secure. Claims that the Register has been manipulated are false, misleading and unsupported by evidence. The Commission condemns such misleading claims and urges all stakeholders to refrain from spreading misinformation and disinformation. Polling stations will open at 6:00 a.m. and close at 5:00 p.m. Where polling commences later than scheduled due to unforeseen circumstances, the lost time will be compensated to ensure that voters receive the full polling period. All voters who are in the queue by 5:00 p.m. will be allowed to cast their ballots. Taking photographs or recording images of marked ballot papers inside the polling booth is strictly prohibited and constitutes an election offence under Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act, No. 37 of 2016. The Commission, in close collaboration with the National Police Service, has put in place adequate security arrangements to ensure a peaceful and orderly electoral process. Two uniformed police officers will be deployed at every polling station, while additional officers will be stationed at tallying centres to maintain law and order and safeguard the integrity of the election. All political parties, candidates, agents and supporters are reminded that compliance with the Electoral Code of Conduct is mandatory. The Commission will not hesitate to invoke all enforcement measures provided for under the Electoral Code of Conduct without fear or favour. The Commission's investigation team is actively investigating all alleged violations with a view to fully enforcing the Code. The Commission calls upon voters, political parties, candidates, observers, civil society organizations and members of the public to report any electoral offence or breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct. Members of the public are encouraged to REPORT and PROVIDE evidence of any electoral malpractice to the Commission, the National Police Service or any other authorized investigative agency. The Commission remains steadfast in its commitment to delivering a peaceful, free, fair, transparent and credible election whose outcome reflects the freely expressed will of the people. Registered voters of Ol Kalou Constituency: Your vote is your voice. Turn out in large numbers, cast your ballot and peacefully shape the future of your constituency. title: IEBC Launches Strategic Plan 2024 2029 and Election Operations Plan 2025 202724th Jun 2026
text: Today marks a significant milestone in Kenya’s democratic space as the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) launches the Strategic Plan 2024–2029 and Election Operations Plan (EOP) 2025–2027, setting a clear roadmap towards stronger electoral governance, institutional excellence, and enhanced public trust. The Plan, themed “Inclusion and Participation in Deepening Democracy in Kenya,” sets out the Commission’s priorities and strategic actions aimed at strengthening electoral management, enhancing citizen participation, promoting equitable representation, and building institutional resilience. The IEBC Strategic Plan 2024–2029 provides a clear roadmap for strengthening Kenya’s electoral democracy over the next five years. Developed through an inclusive and participatory process, the Plan outlines the Commission’s priorities, strategic actions, and measurable targets aimed at enhancing transparency, accountability, and public confidence in the electoral system. The Chief Guest, Martha Koome, FCIArb, EGH, Chief Justice of the Republic of Kenya , said she was honoured and privileged to join the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) for the launch of the Strategic Plan 2024–2029 and the Election Operations Plan 2025–2027, which is an extract of the Strategic Plan detailing how the various strategies will be implemented. She noted that the launch marks a significant milestone in Kenya’s collective journey towards strengthening democracy, enhancing electoral governance, and deepening citizen participation. Chief Justice Koome observed that the Strategic Plan comes at a critical time in the nation’s democratic development. She emphasized that elections are not merely events conducted on polling day but constitute a continuous process that requires strong institutions, adequate resources, effective planning, and a sound and enabling legal framework. She expressed encouragement that the Strategic Plan identifies strengthening the electoral legal framework as a key strategic priority. According to the Chief Justice, harmonizing electoral laws and regulations is both timely and necessary to eliminate inconsistencies, address legal gaps identified during previous electoral cycles, and provide greater clarity to all electoral stakeholders. She noted the need to ensure that electoral timelines, dispute resolution mechanisms, and election management processes are clearly defined and understood. The Chief Justice further noted that the Strategic Plan recognizes the growing role of technology in electoral management. She observed that technology has become an indispensable tool for enhancing efficiency, transparency, and accountability in electoral processes. However, she cautioned that technology alone cannot guarantee credibility and that its effectiveness depends on robust legal safeguards, institutional oversight, and the willingness of all stakeholders to embrace and trust technological systems. Koome emphasized the need for legal frameworks that adequately address data protection, cybersecurity, transparency in electoral technologies, and accountability in electronic electoral processes. She noted that the Commission must provide clear guidance on the deployment, management, and auditing of electoral technologies to ensure innovation strengthens rather than undermines public confidence in elections. She commended the Plan’s commitment to inclusion and equal political participation, noting that the strength of any democracy is measured not only by the conduct of elections but also by the extent to which all citizens can participate meaningfully in the electoral process. She emphasized that women, youth, persons with disabilities, minority communities, and other marginalized groups must be active participants and beneficiaries of democracy. The Chief Justice underscored the importance of public trust, noting that citizens must have confidence that electoral processes are fair, transparent, inclusive, and governed by laws that are applied consistently and impartially. She stated that public trust cannot be demanded but must be earned through integrity, accountability, and continuous improvement. Koome further observed that strengthening democracy in Kenya is not the responsibility of the Commission alone but a national endeavour requiring commitment, cooperation, and goodwill from all sectors of society. She called on all stakeholders to work together in building an electoral system that delivers elections that are free, fair, trusted, inclusive, peaceful, and reflective of the sovereign will of the people. In conclusion, the Chief Justice stated that the true measure of the Strategic Plan will not be found solely in the activities undertaken or resources invested, but in the confidence it inspires among citizens and the extent to which it strengthens the credibility of elections in Kenya. She called upon all Kenyans to support the Commission and help create a safe and conducive environment for nurturing and strengthening the country’s democracy. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said that by unveiling these two strategic documents, the Commission has set in motion a deliberate, transparent and accountable journey towards the 2027 General Election. He noted that the launch reaffirms the Commission’s constitutional mandate, institutional resolve and solemn duty to protect and uphold the sovereign will of the people of Kenya. The IEBC Strategic Plan is anchored on the theme, “Inclusion and Participation in Deepening Democracy in Kenya,” under the clarion call, “Your Vote, Your Voice – Kura Yako, Sauti Yako.” It sets out the Commission’s vision of an electoral management body that is credible, trusted, responsive, and firmly committed to delivering electoral processes that are inclusive, transparent, efficient and accountable. The Strategic Plan is the product of extensive consultations and contributions from stakeholders who helped shape a roadmap that reflects the aspirations of the Kenyan people and gives practical expression to the national values of participation, inclusivity, transparency, accountability and good governance. The Plan identifies four key strategic priorities: effective management of elections, citizen engagement and participation, equitable representation, and strengthened institutional governance. These priorities will guide every decision, reform and action undertaken by the Commission over the next five years. A key component of the launch is the Election Operations Plan 2025–2027. While the Strategic Plan provides the vision and direction, the Election Operations Plan provides the pathway to implementation. It outlines the activities, timelines, responsibilities and milestones that will guide the Commission’s preparations for the 2027 General Election. The Chairperson stated that the Plan demonstrates the Commission’s commitment to early planning, institutional preparedness, transparency and accountability. He emphasized that credible elections do not happen by chance but are built deliberately through careful preparation, sound planning, professional execution and unwavering fidelity to the Constitution and the law. Ethekon assured Kenyans that the Commission has listened to their expectations, reflected on lessons from previous electoral cycles and considered recommendations from election observation missions, court decisions, post-election evaluations and stakeholder engagements. He noted that these lessons have informed the reforms, priorities and operational improvements contained in the documents launched today. He further pledged that the Commission will safeguard the integrity of the electoral process, protect the secrecy and sanctity of every vote, and uphold the sovereign will of the people of Kenya. He expressed the Commission’s desire that when the story of the 2027 General Election is written, Kenyans will say that their Electoral Commission prepared diligently, acted impartially, rose to the occasion and faithfully discharged its constitutional mandate. The Chairperson observed that the success of any election is not the responsibility of the Commission alone. He emphasized that democracy is a shared responsibility whose strength depends on the commitment of all actors, including political parties, candidates, state institutions, the media, civil society, development partners and citizens. He noted that the ballot remains the highest expression of the sovereign will of the people and must be protected collectively, consistently and courageously. Ethekon expressed gratitude to State and non-state agencies for their continued support in strengthening Kenya’s democratic institutions. He also acknowledged the support of development partners, including IFES, ELGIA, UNDP, ECES, International IDEA, Uraia Trust, CMD-Kenya, NIMD, The Carter Center and others who continue to contribute to institutional strengthening and electoral reforms. As the Commission launches these important instruments, the Chairperson called upon all stakeholders to renew their collective commitment to protecting the Constitution, strengthening democratic governance and ensuring that every Kenyan can exercise their democratic rights freely, peacefully, confidently and with dignity. He noted that through collaboration, integrity, professionalism and fidelity to the Constitution, Kenya will deliver electoral processes that honour the aspirations of its people and strengthen the nation’s democratic future. #IEBCStrategicPlan #KuraYakoSautiYako #DeepeningDemocracy

title: Regional Electoral Management Bodies Capacity-Building Programme Concludes in Machakos12th Jun 2026
text: The Regional Electoral Management Bodies (EMBs) Capacity-Building and Experience-Sharing Programme in Machakos County, where the IEBC Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, Commissioners and senior members of staff participated, has successfully concluded. Over the past three days, electoral leaders and senior officials from Kenya, Seychelles, Malawi, and Uganda engaged in insightful discussions on electoral governance, leadership, electoral integrity, stakeholder engagement, emerging technologies, misinformation and disinformation, crisis communication, and dispute resolution. The closing ceremony was presided over by IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, as the host, who reiterated the importance of continuous learning, collaboration, and innovation in strengthening electoral processes across the region. Participants expressed their appreciation to COMESA, EISA, and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) for providing a valuable platform for peer learning and knowledge exchange. They noted that the lessons and best practices gained during the programme will be applied to improve election management in their respective countries.

title: IEBC Participates in Regional EMB Capacity-Building and Experience-Sharing Programme11th Jun 2026
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) is participating in a regional Electoral Management Bodies (EMBs) Capacity-Building and Experience-Sharing Programme taking place in Machakos, Kenya, from 10 to 13 June 2026. The programme, organized under the auspices of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) with technical support from the Electoral Institute for Sustainable Democracy in Africa (EISA), brings together Commissioners and senior electoral officials from Kenya, Seychelles, Malawi, and Uganda to strengthen electoral governance and promote peer learning across the region. The engagement provides a platform for electoral leaders to exchange experiences, share best practices, and discuss emerging challenges affecting election administration in Africa. The discussions focus on strengthening institutional independence, enhancing leadership and decision-making capacities, promoting electoral integrity, and improving stakeholder engagement. A key feature of the programme is the examination of contemporary challenges facing electoral management bodies, including misinformation and disinformation, the growing influence of artificial intelligence and digital technologies in electoral processes, crisis communication, and electoral dispute resolution mechanisms. Speaking during the programme on behalf of the Chairperson, Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana welcomed the programme and termed it timely and enriching. “We have the talent, technology, and we have the patriotic duty to deliver for our people,” said Dr. Alutalala as he officially opened the three-day programme. Dr. Alutalala further emphasized the importance of regional collaboration and knowledge sharing in building resilient electoral institutions capable of delivering credible, transparent, and inclusive elections. Through interactive sessions, expert presentations, case studies, and peer-to-peer learning, participants are exploring practical approaches to addressing common electoral challenges while identifying innovative solutions that can enhance public confidence in electoral processes. The participation of the IEBC underscores the Commission's commitment to continuous institutional learning, professional development, and the adoption of regional best practices that contribute to the effective management of elections and strengthening democracy in Kenya. #16thJulyByelection #KuraYakoSautiYako #IEBCStrategicPlan #IEBCEOP

title: IEBC, UNDP Collaborate to Enhance Electoral Integrity and Preparedness for 20279th Jun 2026
text: The Commission, led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, today attended a meeting of the local Project Appraisal Committee (LPAC) of the UNDP-led Elections Project document to finalise plans for the Elections Basket Fund project ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the meeting, Ethekon thanked the development partners, security agencies, gender, youth and women groups present for their support and noted that an election is not a one-day event but a journey where agencies walk together to help achieve an inclusive, transparent, credible, free and fair election. "This collaboration is important for us to build trust and legitimacy of the electoral processes. It is the framework to support elections and a vehicle to mobilise resources for both technical and financial support in the build-up to the 2027 General Election," said Ethekon. The Elections Project document defines the scope, outcomes, outputs and activities required to be implemented prior to the 2027 General Election. If approved and implemented, it will enhance stakeholder engagement and strengthen efforts towards delivering a transparent and credible election. "Election is a journey and I call upon everyone present here today to act responsibly, be accountable for the resources available and work together to achieve tangible results. This document will be taken to the Attorney General and National Treasury for approval before we sign and implement it. I will follow up on the remaining processes to ensure that it is cleared and approved," said Ethekon. Commissioner Ann Nderitu, CBS, said the Elections Project document is anchored on five priorities arising from the 2025 Needs Assessment Mission, including: participation of youth, women and people living with disabilities; strengthening stakeholder engagement and communication; capacity building and technical assistance; electoral security, preparation and early risk awareness coordination; and information integrity to counter misinformation, disinformation and online harm. UNDP’s Resident Representative Jean-Luc Stalon reiterated their support in ensuring the Commission delivers on its constitutional mandate. UNDP has played a pivotal role over successive elections in supporting Kenya to deepen its democracy by contributing to institutional capacity and electoral integrity. LPAC is a mandatory review mechanism where key national partners and concerned UN agencies formally evaluate the project's design, budget availability and technical alignment. The expected outcome is a formal endorsement of the project document before submission to the Office of the Attorney General and National Treasury for approval. #16thJulyByelection #KuraYakoSautiYako #IEBCStrategicPlan #IEBCEOP

title: IEBC and Law Society of Kenya Strengthen Collaboration to Support Credible Electoral Processes9th Jun 2026
text: The Commission, led by Erastus Ethekon, today held a consultative meeting with the leadership of the Law Society of Kenya (LSK), led by its President, Charles Kanjama, SC. The meeting discussed areas of collaboration aimed at strengthening electoral processes. The Chairperson, Erastus Ethekon, welcomed LSK’s commitment to support electoral processes and noted that effective elections depend on strong partnerships with key stakeholders in voter education, strategic communication and institutional coordination. “Sustained collaboration between the Commission and stakeholders remains central to strengthening electoral processes and enhancing public confidence in democratic governance. The Commission intends to enhance structured collaboration frameworks, including the establishment of joint technical teams to support stakeholder engagement and improve coordination in election preparedness activities. In addition, there is a need to review past electoral processes and share lessons learned to strengthen future planning, improve electoral outcomes and build public trust in the electoral system,” said Ethekon. The President of the LSK, Charles Kanjama, SC, reaffirmed the Society’s commitment to supporting free, fair and credible elections. He observed that elections involve a broad ecosystem of actors, including security agencies, political parties, constitutional commissions and legal professionals. Kanjama commended the IEBC for continued collaboration in the conduct of LSK elections over the years and noted that the Society has experienced minimal electoral disputes during this period. He further acknowledged the contribution of legal professionals serving within the Commission and other institutions in strengthening democratic governance. Kanjama said LSK intends to establish a dedicated elections committee to enhance engagement with IEBC and support continuous electoral preparedness and legal reform discussions. He reaffirmed LSK’s commitment to working collaboratively with IEBC and other electoral stakeholders to advance free, fair, transparent and credible elections. #16thJulyByelection #KuraYakoSautiYako #IEBCStrategicPlan #IEBCEOP

title: IEBC Engages MSMEs and Boda Boda Associations on Voter Education Ahead of 2027 General Election29th May 2026
text: Today, IEBC, led by Deputy Commission Secretary – Operations, Ruth Kulundu, met with representatives from the Biashara Ndogo Association of Kenya and the BodaBoda Association of Kenya to explore collaboration opportunities on voter education ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the meeting, Kulundu recognized the critical role MSMEs play in Kenya’s economy and applauded the Associations for proactively seeking partnership with IEBC in strengthening civic and voter education across the country. Kulundu further emphasized that boda boda riders can play a transformative role as ambassadors of peace during the electioneering period, helping to foster national cohesion and responsible civic engagement ahead of the 2027 General Election. Marcos Mwangi, Chairman of the Biashara Ndogo Association of Kenya, affirmed that the Association is non-partisan and committed to empowering its members through voter education and access to voter registration services at the grassroots level. He stressed the importance of equipping citizens with accurate information to enable informed electoral participation. Charles M. Gichira, National Chairman of the BodaBoda Association of Kenya, reiterated the sector’s commitment to promoting peace and changing negative perceptions often associated with elections. He noted that the partnership with IEBC would create platforms for voter education and voter registration during the Association’s engagements and meetings across the country.

title: IEBC Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, Leads IEBC Team in 2027 Budget Presentation to JLAC14th May 2026
text: The Commission, led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, appeared before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs (JLAC) on May 12th 2026, chaired by Hon. title: IEBC Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Joins African Dialogue on Election Observer Accreditation12th May 2026
text: Today, IEBC Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication and Stakeholder Engagement Committee, attended a Joint Dialogue on Citizen Election Observer Accreditation in Africa. The event brought together senior electoral commissioners and directors from Election Management Bodies (EMBs) in Ghana, Malawi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Nigeria, and Kenya to discuss strengthening accreditation frameworks for citizen election observers across the continent. While opening the roundtable discussion, Dr. Mukhwana noted that elections in Africa attract enormous public interest and expectation. He emphasized that election observation is no longer a ceremonial addition to the democratic process, but an integral part of electoral integrity. He added that the presence of observers helps simplify and communicate complex electoral processes to the public, thereby enhancing transparency, accountability, and trust in electoral administration. He further observed that EMBs and observer groups continue to face challenges such as administrative friction, scalability, and technological changes. He stated that IEBC is currently undertaking efforts to modernize its accreditation management systems, adding that such dialogues provide an important platform for progressive solutions and institutional reform. Dr. Alutalala underscored that despite differing national experiences, the shared objective remains the establishment of a gold standard for accreditation that balances the integrity and security of electoral processes with inclusivity and openness. He concluded by stressing that true democratic fidelity requires grassroots civil society organizations, community networks, and observer groups to have a place at the national democratic table. Mr. Richard Klein, Global Director for Elections at the National Democratic Institute (NDI), noted that EMBs and non-partisan citizen election observers have both built significant capacity over the past four decades in promoting credible elections. He added that while accreditation is intended to support transparent, participatory, and accountable elections, global trends show that the process is becoming increasingly complex, creating challenges for both EMBs and observer groups. The event serves as a platform for constructive networking and engagement between EMBs and citizen observer groups, reaffirming non-partisan citizen observation as a cornerstone of transparent and accountable elections across Africa.

title: JLAC Convenes Key Institutions to Strengthen 2027 Election Preparedness31st Mar 2026
text: Today, the Departmental Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs (JLAC) held a joint stakeholder engagement bringing together IEBCK, Judiciary, the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP), and the Witness Protection Agency (WPA). In his welcoming remarks, Hon. George Gitonga Murugara, CBS, MP (Tharaka Constituency) and Chairperson of JLAC, reaffirmed the Committee’s unwavering support for the Commission. title: IEBC Targets 2.5 Million New Voters in Enhanced Registration Drive30th Mar 2026
text: The Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration exercise will take place in the 30,619 gazetted registration centers countrywide that include the 57 Huduma centers. A kit movement schedule will be prepared in consultation with relevant stakeholders to determine how the kit will move around the County Assembly ward for the ECVR period. The Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) exercise targets to register approximately 2.5 million new voters. The exercise will bring registration services closer to citizens by moving from constituency offices to ward level and institutions of higher learning. The exercise targets to increase coverage by expanding enrollment, particularly for first-time registrants and youth, especially in under-registered or remote areas and also enhance inclusivity and equity to facilitate broader participation among marginalized groups. The Commission will make arrangements to have kits for universities and institutions of higher learning, in electoral areas where they are located to cater for students studying away from their home areas. Students are therefore not required to travel back home to be listed as voters. The registration kits stationed at the 57 Huduma Centers countrywide will be open such that anyone who wishes to register for the first time will be allowed to select a registration center of their choice and their details captured to the selected center. This will save Kenyans the trouble of having to travel long distances so as to be registered as a voter. The Commission will seek inter-agency collaboration by partnering with agencies like the National Registration Bureau (NRB) to fast-track the issuance of IDs, which are a legal prerequisite for voter registration. The requirement for one to be registered as a voter is that they should be a Kenyan citizen of majority age and with a national identification card or valid passport. The individual must present themselves physically to a registration officer as the registration process involves capturing biometric features and personal identifiable details of the applicant. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFutureYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

The Commission shall issue a separate notice on voter registration and revision of the register for citizens residing outside the country and for prisoners. Registration of voters at Huduma Centers shall continue after the lapse of the period provided for conduct of ECVR and shall be suspended by notice by the Commission. Voters are further notified that at the conclusion of ECVR, the Commission will resume continuous voter registration at the respective Constituency offices. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFutureYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: Launch of ECVR30th Mar 2026
text: Today Monday 30th March 2026, the Commission is launching a nationwide Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration drive that shall run up to Tuesday 28th April 2026. The launch is happening at Shimoni Village – Old Jetty Grounds (Shimoni Fish Port) in Lunga Lunga Constituency in Kwale County. The exercise targets new registration for all, transfers and change of particulars. The #ECVR2026 exercise will be conducted at the County Assembly Wards (CAW) on a rotational basis in accordance with approved kit movement schedules as well as Institutions of Higher Learning, Huduma Ceners, Constituency Offices, Huduma Centers, and at the Commission’s Customer Experience Center (Ground Floor, Anniversary Towers). The ward-based decentralization ECVR is shifting registration from constituency offices to the ward levels to reduce travel distances for citizens in remote and rural areas. There will be a minimum of three kits per ward to ensure universal basic coverage and an additional kit will be deployed to constituencies where projected registration targets exceed their monthly capacity. Registration is open to Kenyan citizens who have attained the age of eighteen (18) years and are in possession of a valid Kenyan Passport and National Identity Card. Continuous voter registration and revision of the register shall NOT be undertaken in electoral areas with scheduled By-Elections or ongoing election petitions. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFutureYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC, Media Stakeholders Sign MoU to Strengthen Election Reporting Ahead of 202727th Mar 2026
text: The Commission today held a breakfast meeting on Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (EVCR) and signing of the memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) and the Kenya Media Sector Working Group (KMSWG), which is a coalition of key media stakeholders. Speaking during the launch, Commission Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, who was accompanied by Members of the Commission, said the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) solidifies partnership in election reporting. “We have significant tasks ahead of us, particularly the management of the 2027 General Election. We are currently preparing for the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR), which will be launched on March 30, 2026, in Shimoni, Kwale County. Timely access to electoral information will be a priority, and IEBC will provide accurate and timely updates on all election-related matters during the electoral calendar we are currently implementing. We will also grant access to all polling centres and tallying centres for accredited journalists, who will receive training to understand their duties. We will create a platform for collaboration to explain to Kenyans how results are transmitted from polling stations to constituency tallying centers and ultimately to the national tallying center, to alleviate any anxiety in society. We agree on the importance of factchecking and holding the media accountable to verify information before publishing and broadcasting. “To the media, I urge you to go out and capture the stories of the ECVR and all other electoral processes, from the remotest villages in our country to the cities. Remember, this is our country, and we all have a role to play in making democracy work. Together, let us be objective and factual in our engagement and reporting. Let us encourage every Kenyan aged 18 and above, especially the youth, to register to vote. Let us promote peace throughout the electoral cycle violence has no place in democracy,” said Ethekon. We must all be accountable for our actions, as both the media and the IEBC. Those who call for accountability from the IEBC should also reflect on their own actions. Accountability is a two-way street, and everyone must play their part. Eric Oduor, the Kenya Union of Journalist Secretary General cautioned on the anticipated increase in disinformation and misinformation in the lead up to the 2027 General Election. He said the Commission needs to interact with the media in ways that go beyond just news gathering and reporting. “We hope that through our partnership, IEBC will set up a media centre with a fact-checking desk where journalists can work to counter fake news,” said Oduor. Kenya Editors Guild (KEG) President Zubeida Kananu said that free press and transparency at IEBC are values worth investing in and that the landscape of 2027 is a digital jungle. The landscape involves not only TV, radio and print media but also TikTok, Facebook, X (twitter), and the rise of alternative media. “We must also prepare for the 'Deepfake Election.' This MoU is not merely a peer contract. We expect the Commission to provide accurate information at the right time to dispel rumours before they spread. We have agreed on the rules of engagement and have chosen a partnership based on integrity over convenience,” said Kananu. Lilian Mahiri-Zaja, a member of the Elgia Afric Board, said the media serves as a mediator, ensuring that the public is engaged, which helps build trust in the electoral process and supports the IEBC in fulfilling its mandate. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: ORPP, IRI and IEBC Lead Dialogue Summit on Youth Engagement in Political Processes24th Mar 2026
text: Today, the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORRP) is hosting the Youth and Political Parties Dialogue Summit in Nairobi. Opening the summit, John Cox Lorionokou, the Registrar of Political Parties, highlighted that "Kenya’s youth are not disengaged, they are redefining participation. He affirmed that the Commission will strictly enforce legal requirements, including the two-thirds gender principle and compliance in party nomination lists, cautioning that non-compliant lists will be rejected to safeguard electoral integrity. Regarding youth participation, the Chairperson noted that the Commission aims to register over 6.3 new voters ahead of the 2027 General Election. text: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) with support from Elgia, convened a multi-sectoral workshop in February 2026 bringing together key stakeholders to deliberate on the proposed electoral legal reforms. title: Commissioner Ann Nderitu, CBS Rallies Youth at Evangelical Leaders Congress18th Mar 2026
text: As part of its ongoing stakeholder engagement efforts, Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) was today represented by Commissioner Dr Ann Nderitu, CBS, at the Leaders Congress of the Evangelical Youth Alliance. Speaking on ‘The Place of Youth and Religious Institutions in Building Democracy’, Commissioner Dr Nderitu delivered a timely and necessary message on youth participation in elections. “Young people must move beyond passive observation and actively engage in the democratic process by registering as voters, turning out on election day, contesting for leadership positions, applying for poll official roles and using their influence across social media and creative platforms such as music, poetry and spoken word to promote voter education awareness,” she noted. She further highlighted the importance of youth contributing to voter education, participating in legal reform processes, supporting peaceful elections and leveraging available opportunities such as AGPO to be part of the electoral ecosystem. Drawing from recent electoral data, she noted that while 3,430 youth contested in 2017 with 314 elected, and 4,350 contested in 2022 with 335 elected, the increase in participation had not translated proportionately into leadership outcomes. Notably, there were no youth presidential or deputy presidential candidates in 2022, despite youth remaining the largest demographic. She underscored a persistent paradox that while young people hold significant demographic power, the power is often underutilized, misunderstood or even suppressed. The real issue is not numbers, but the gap between potential and actual participation, which ultimately determines electoral outcomes. Commissioner Nderitu reaffirmed the critical role of the Church in election management and democratic governance, from promoting accountability and political tolerance to fostering national cohesion, peace building, and active participation in election observation, while maintaining non-partisanship. As the Commission plans to launch Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) on 30th March 2026, bringing registration services closer to communities and institutions of higher learning, Commissioner Nderitu called upon every eligible young person to come out and register. "If you have an ID, register, participate, and use your voice—because the future of leadership and governance in this country will be shaped by those who choose to show up." #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: Commission Prepares for ECVR with Structured Nationwide Training Programme16th Mar 2026
text: In preparation for the upcoming Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) scheduled to begin on 30th March 2026, the Commission has adopted a structured cascaded training model. Through this strategy, the Commission will deploy additional voter registration kits, and employ Voter Registration Assistants, Voter Registration Clerks and ICT Clerks. title: Commission Joins CUEA Cultural Week to Advance Youth Electoral Participation14th Mar 2026
text: IEBC Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson – Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication & Stakeholder Engagement Committee, representing Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC is presiding over The Catholic University of Eastern Africa - CUEA #CulturalWeek2026 to celebrate the institution’s cultural diversity and lead discussions on the electoral process, specifically voter registration among the young people. “It is a profound honor for the Commission to stand among you tonight. Over five hundred of you have registered to vote! Congratulations! We have spent the last few days witnessing the "Threads of Culture" that define this great institution. From the rhythm of the drums to the brilliance of the Fashion Show and the richness of African Cuisines, you have shown that culture is not just a memory of the past—it is a living, breathing identity. "Threads of Culture: Bridging Identity Through Generations," is powerful. Culture is the foundation upon which we build our society through identity, unity and legacy. Since time immemorial, our ancestors used cultural gatherings to choose leaders, resolve conflicts and plan for the future. Today, that "cultural gathering" has evolved into the democratic process. The Missing Thread: Your Voice in the 2027 Elections. As we admire the beautiful Ankara fabrics and the traditional performances tonight, we must ask ourselves: What is the most important way to protect our heritage? It is by choosing leaders who value it. We are heading toward the 2027 General Elections. Currently, the IEBC is conducting Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) across all 290 constituencies. However, we have a challenge. While 75% of Kenyans are under the age of 35, voter enrollment among university students remains low. title: IEBC, KMSWG Hold Workshop to Review MOU Between IEBC and the Media10th Mar 2026
text: Today Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson – Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication & Stakeholder Engagement Committee, brought together the Kenya Media Sector Working Group for a Workshop on Review of the MOU Between IEBC and the Media. Dr. Alutalala opened the workshop by highlighting the importance of a trust-based relationship between the media and IEBC. He noted that the media is critical in helping citizens understand how elections work, and countering dis/misinformation that can overshadow facts. Dr. Alutalala emphasized that restoring public confidence is as crucial as personal integrity and that elections begin long before polling day, “Help the public understand the work we do. Help them see the role of an electoral administrator. The media is essential in rebuilding public confidence in our democratic process,” he said. This MOU is more than a document. It’s a framework for partnership, a tool to empower journalists, and a pathway to a transparent, credible and inclusive election in 2027. Moses Sunkuli, OGW, Ag. Commission Secretary/CEO reflected on lessons from past elections, emphasizing that elections are a continuous process. Journalists must understand every stage—from voter registration and verification to results transmission—to ensure accurate reporting. “As we prepare for the 2027 General Election, this engagement is both timely and necessary. Elections take place within a dynamic information environment where facts, narratives and public trust interact and shape public perception. In that space, the partnership between the electoral management body and the media is indispensable,” he said. Felix Oduor, Executive Director, ELGIA, highlighted the historical role of media in Kenya’s electoral process, noting that collaborative engagement between electoral bodies and the media has precedent both locally and internationally. He emphasized that such partnerships enhance transparency and public trust, citing examples from previous elections and comparative experiences from Ghana and the United States. Felix stressed that while challenges exist, particularly around timing and coordination, a well-structured framework for media engagement can significantly strengthen electoral integrity and ensure that the public receives accurate, timely information. Zubeidah Kananu, President of KEG, emphasized the diversity of the media sector and the responsibility it carries. "Through this MOU, we ensure journalists are trained, informed, and ready to report elections responsibly, minimizing misinformation and conflict,", she noted. Martin Maasai, Trustee at KEG and Chairperson of the Media Freedoms & Ethics Committee, reflected on the current state of the media industry, noting the rapid turnover of experienced journalists and the prevalence of younger reporters covering elections for the first time. He stressed the importance of creating spaces for engagement and training between the media and the IEBC, ensuring journalists understand the full electoral process—from voter registration to the announcement of results. Maasai emphasized that responsible and informed reporting is essential for transparency, public confidence and preventing misinformation, reminding participants that “journalists do what they do precisely because they care about this country.” Victor Bwire, Director of Media Training and Development, MCK, highlighted the collaborative efforts already underway between MCK and IEBC to train journalists on electoral processes and responsible election reporting. He noted the challenges posed by Kenya’s vast media landscape, with hundreds of radio, TV, digital and blog platforms, emphasizing that standardized training and clear guidelines are essential for consistent, accurate coverage. Bwire also spoke on emerging issues like artificial intelligence, digital media, and user-generated content, explaining that the new Code of Ethics and the “Introduction to Media Practice” course aim to equip all media practitioners—including non-journalists—with the skills to report ethically and professionally. He concluded by stressing that coordinated reporting, journalist safety, and adherence to standards are critical for enhancing public trust and credibility in elections. The workshop reinforced the partnership between IEBC and the media, ensuring journalists are equipped to safeguard credible, transparent and peaceful elections in 2027.

title: IEBC, CMD Engages Citizens at the 8th Peoples Dialogue Festival (PDF)4th Mar 2026
text: Today, Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), led by Erastus Ethekon, addressed participants at the 8th People’s Dialogue Festival, held at Uhuru Park from 4th – 7th March 2026, reflecting on Kenya’s democratic challenges while expressing confidence in its continued progress. “It is both an honour and a responsibility to stand at Uhuru Park, a space deeply woven into Kenya’s democratic journey. Democracy is not sustained by institutions alone. It is sustained by participation, by trust, and above all, by people especially our youth,” said Ethekon. Erastus Ethekon underscored the urgency on boundary delimitation, matter, calling for structured and inclusive dialogue anchored in constitutional and legal frameworks. While acknowledging that the courts may pronounce themselves on specific issues, he emphasized that sustainable solutions require consensus-building and public confidence through open engagement. Turning to campaign financing and the cost of elections, he spoke frankly about the financial realities of administering credible, transparent, and verifiable elections. However, he cautioned that beyond administrative expenses, the escalating cost of political campaigns poses a deeper democratic risk. “Excessive and unregulated spending breeds inequality and creates fertile ground for malpractice,” he noted. Ethekon called for stronger transparency and accountability mechanisms. Addressing recent incidents of violence during by-elections, he firmly rejected the notion that intimidation equates to democratic participation. “We have witnessed disturbing scenes individuals armed with crude weapons, allegedly in the name of protecting their democratic rights. That is not democracy,” he stated. “ He said democracy must be safeguarded through institutions, dialogue, and respect for the rule of law not through violence. With the launch of a nationwide enhanced continuous voter registration exercise on 30th March 2026, the Chairperson placed particular focus on young Kenyans. He expressed confidence in their judgment, energy, and collective strength, reminding them that their power lies in their numbers. “You do not need any more power than that,” he said. “Register. Participate. This is not merely a right it is a civic duty and responsibility.” On security and peace, he was unequivocal: credible elections cannot take place in an environment devoid of stability. He challenged stakeholders present to move beyond rhetoric and ask the hard questions about how to create and safeguard a peaceful electoral environment. “That is the honest, forward-looking dialogue we must continue to have,” he remarked. Reflecting on the Commission’s renewed direction, the Chairman described the current IEBC as representing a paradigm shift. He observed that, unlike in the past when many citizens only became familiar with electoral leaders at the point of results declaration, the Commission has deliberately chosen openness from the outset. Since assuming office, the leadership has engaged youth in Kirinyaga, Machakos, and Nairobi, met with media, civil society, political parties, and development partners many present at the Festival. “We are fostering a culture of accessibility and transparency,” he said. “We are committed to being visible, accessible, and accountable.” He further proposed that forums such as the People’s Dialogue Festival be extended to counties across the country, with the Commission actively participating to dismantle outdated narratives that portray it as distant or opaque. “That narrative must become a thing of the past,” he affirmed. He pledged that the Commission would plan early, communicate early, and engage consistently. “We will explain ourselves clearly. We will tell our story every step of the way. That is our commitment to you especially to the young people of this country.” At the same time, he emphasized that elections cannot be delivered by one institution alone. The Commission will depend on collaboration with development partners, sister commissions, political parties, civil society, universities, colleges, and citizens at large. “Elections are a collective responsibility. We must all be involved. We must all be accountable. And together, we must safeguard our democracy.” In closing, the Chairperson urged Kenyans not to allow negativity to eclipse progress. He described Kenya’s democracy as resilient and evolving not broken. He highlighted the country’s advanced voter register, consistent deployment of electoral technology since 2013, and robust legal framework as areas of regional and global recognition. International electoral bodies across Africa and Asia, he noted, frequently seek to learn from Kenya’s experience, benchmarking its systems and reforms. “So let us not dwell only on our shortcomings. Let us also acknowledge the tremendous reforms we have undertaken, the institutions we have built, and the resilience we have demonstrated as a nation. Our democracy is a work in progress, but it is a strong one, and together, we will continue perfecting it,” he concluded. #FormNiDialogue #YourVoteYourFuture #TalkwithIEBC #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC Holds Planning Meeting for Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration2nd Mar 2026
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon is holding a planning meeting for the forthcoming Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR). The meeting aims to provide strategic direction on the national rollout of the exercise; clarify roles, responsibilities and coordination frameworks between field officers and headquarters teams, and legal & procedural guidelines; identify operational risks and formulate appropriate mitigation measures; develop a monitoring, evaluation and reporting framework with clearly defined performance indicators and shape a unified public communication and stakeholder engagement strategy for the ECVR period. The planned EVCR will commence on 30th March 2026 across the country for 30 days. The target is 2.5 million new voter registrations during Phase One of the ECVR exercise. The Commission projects a register of at least 6.3 million new voters to hit its projected target of 28.5 million voters in for the 2027 General Election. “The ECVR is one of the initiatives of fulfilling a constitutional obligation. Our fundamental objective is to ensure that every eligible Kenyan citizen can exercise their right to vote. The credibility of any electoral process begins with an inclusive, accurate and trusted Register of Voter,” said Ethekon. Further, the Chairperson observed that voter registration is a constitutional guarantee. Our responsibility is to make this exercise practical and accessible to all. IEBC is shifting from a passive model to a proactive one. By engaging temporary voter registration clerks, the Commission is deliberately bringing voter registration services to the people. The personnel will travel from village to village delivering registration services directly to the people. “Registration will be decentralized to the lowest feasible administrative levels and must also direct special attention and resources to remote, marginalized and hard-to-reach areas. Our approach must be adaptive to geographical and infrastructural challenges. No Kenyan should be excluded because of where they live,” said Ethekon. The Chairperson concluded by observing that ECVR exercise must be transparent, accountable and conducted with the highest standards of professionalism from recruitment of clerks and logistics until the data uploads of new enrollments. All personnel involved in the ECVR exercise must uphold the highest standards of integrity. “We are trustees of public confidence. Every action we take must reflect that responsibility,” Ethekon noted. Commissioner Dr Ann Nderitu, CBS, the Chairperson, Electoral Operations Committee said the target of 2.5 million voters over the next 30 days is grounded on demographic realities, particularly the large cohort of youth who have attained voting age since the last mass registration cycle. The credibility and inclusiveness of the 2027 electoral process will depend significantly on the Register we build today. She noted that the success of ECVR rests on three interdependent pillars; training, logistics and stakeholder engagement where emphasis will be placed on practical competency particularly biometric capture quality, kit operation, data transmission and troubleshooting in low-connectivity environments. Commissioner Nderitu urged that there should be strict adherence to the kit movement schedule to ensure timely rotation across wards and centres within the limited timeframe and real-time monitoring, rapid issue resolution and strong field supervision will be essential throughout the exercise. Ag. Commission Secretary/CEO Moses Sunkuli, OGW said ECVR will base its foundation on active network connectivity, logistic and compliance to data protection laws and urged staff to plan well by identifying the risks, challenges, and propose solutions going forward. “The Commission needs to ensure that network connectivity is up and running and any challenges still remaining are dealt with and given priority so that all our process and activities are supported by the network to make sure transfers and voter registration is real time. “From our past challenges, you are encouraged to come up with strategies that are accurate and consistent for registration of data. The voter education strategies must be purposefully designed to make sure all voters are educated and @IEBCKenya is able to receive interractive feedback. Lets go all out to engage and ensure all people participate,” Sunkuli said.

title: IEBC and CMD Kenya Host Youth Dialogue Forum in Kirinyaga County26th Feb 2026
text: The IEBC led by Commissioners Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana and Ann Nderitu, CBS, in collaboration with the Centre for Multiparty Democracy, Kenya, today held a Youth Dialogue Forum in Kirinyaga County. The forum brought together over 200 young people and was graced by the Member of Parliament for Kirinyaga Central Constituency and host, Hon. Joseph Gachoki Gitari, Hussein Allasow and the County Commissioner for Kirinyaga. The Member of Parliament for Kirinyaga Central Constituency and host, Hon. Joseph Gachoki Gitari commended the Commission for strengthening public confidence in Kenya’s constitutional order. He particularly praised IEBC for its professionalism and dedication during the recently concluded by elections, noting that by elections are complex national exercises that require thorough preparation, effective coordination, transparency and firmness of character. He called on all stakeholders to uphold peaceful electoral processes, stressing that acts of hooliganism and violence that undermine democracy must be firmly rejected. He concluded by underscoring that elections must always be conducted in accordance with the law and that their outcomes must reflect the free will of the people. Commissioner Alutalala who is the Chairperson, Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication and Stakeholder Engagement Committee observed that there is often a perceived tension between young people and the older generation, with narratives suggesting that the youth are energetic and fast moving while older leaders are viewed as outdated or disconnected. He described such perceptions as worrying, emphasizing that both youth and experience are valuable. He noted that while youth is a spark full of energy, wisdom is a steady flame, and the two must complement each other rather than compete. The Commissioner assured participants that the Commission was present to listen. He encouraged them to speak candidly about what they would like the Commission to improve or address. He added that he would take note of their concerns so that there could be meaningful responses and continued dialogue. He urged the youth to seek accurate information about electoral processes and avoid spreading misinformation, cautioning that being misinformed can mislead others. He emphasized the importance of continuous engagement, verification of information and constructive participation in democratic processes. Commissioner Ann Nderitu stated that the engagement was focused on elections and enhancing young people’s participation in governance, particularly through voter registration. She emphasized that registration as a voter is the first and most important step in participating in governance. She urged young people not only to register but also mobilize their peers who are not yet registered, stressing that meaningful participation in governance begins with being a registered voter. She reiterated earlier remarks that youth is a stage in life and part of a natural progression. She noted that everyone is born a child, grows into youth, and later matures into adulthood. She called on young people to respect older generations, observing that older individuals have experienced stages of life that the youth are yet to go through. At the same time, she acknowledged that each generation faces different circumstances and opportunities. The Commissioner encouraged young people to make productive use of their youthful years, describing them as foundational and energy filled years that should be invested wisely. She cautioned against wasting this critical period, noting that failure to build a strong foundation could perpetuate cycles of poverty and disadvantage into the next generation. She urged them to take responsibility for shaping both their personal futures and that of the country. IEBC Ag Commission Secretary/CEO Moses Sunkuli, OGW, thanked the young people for their strong turnout, stating that it was a great honour and privilege to engage with the youth of Kenya and Kirinyaga County. He noted that the forum was not just another meeting, but a call to action, adding that vijana wanawajibika na wameamua kuchukua hatua mwafaka. He observed that young people form the largest voting bloc in the country and are the most connected generation, describing them as the most powerful force in shaping the direction of Kenya’s democracy. He emphasized that the future of the country will not be determined without them, but by them. The CEO expressed sincere appreciation to the Centre for Multiparty Democracy Kenya for sponsoring and supporting the engagement. He acknowledged the organisation’s commitment to strengthening democratic participation, especially among young people, noting that its efforts play a critical role in deepening Kenya’s democratic culture. He further commended the partnership and called for continued collaboration to achieve shared objectives. He informed participants that the Commission has advertised temporary positions for the upcoming Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration exercise, including Voter Registration Assistants, Registration Clerks and ICT Clerks. He described these opportunities as a chance to safeguard democracy and encouraged young people to apply and take an active role in the electoral process. The CEO also called on all eligible young people aged 18 years and above who have not registered as voters to do so, noting that Continuous Voter Registration is ongoing and that the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration exercise will soon be launched. He encouraged them not only to register, but also to mobilize their friends, classmates and colleagues to register, stressing that democracy grows stronger when young people participate fully in all electoral processes. Addressing the role of digital platforms, he cautioned against the rapid spread of misinformation and urged the youth to use their online platforms responsibly by sharing verified information, challenging false narratives and contributing to an informed and confident electorate. In conclusion, he noted that the 2027 General Election is fast approaching and encouraged them to embrace meaningful participation and youth leadership, reminding them that democracy, the future and responsibility belong to them. #26thFebByelections | #YourVoteYourFuture | #TalkwithIEBC | #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC Appears Before JLAC to Consider 2026 Budget Policy Statement25th Feb 2026
text: The Commission, led by IEBC Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat, OGW, appeared before the Departmental Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs (JLAC) at Bunge Towers to consider the 2026 Budget Policy Statement (BPS). Vice Chairperson Araphat emphasized to the Committee that timely and sufficient funding is critical to protecting the integrity, efficiency and credibility of Kenya’s electoral process as the country prepares for the 2027 General Election. title: Press release - Collaboration with State Agencies on Managing the Register of Voters16th Feb 2026
text: Nairobi, Kenya: 16th February 2026 The Commission notes with concern recent statements by Democratic Party (DP) regarding IEBC’s engagement with National Registration Bureau in relation to voter registration data and identity verification. Article 88(4) of the Constitution of Kenya and Sections 4 and 6 of the Elections Act, 2011 mandate the Commission to, among other functions, register voters, maintain an accurate and up-to-date register of voters and ensure the integrity and accuracy of the register. Further, Article 249(2)(b) of the Constitution guarantees the Commission’s independence and provides that constitutional commissions shall not be subject to direction or control by any person or authority. In fulfilling this constitutional and statutory mandate, the Commission requires to work with relevant government agencies that are the lawful custodians of lawful and relevant data to the execution of its mandate. This includes collaboration with the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services to make registration of voters efficient and inclusive in line with our mandate. In particular, The National Registration Bureau: To verify national identity card details and eligibility of citizens during voter registration to ensure the accuracy of the register of voters. Civil Registration Services: To confirm death records for lawful removal of deceased persons from the register of voters. The Directorate of Immigration Services: To verify passport details, noting that a Kenyan passport is one of the statutory identification documents permissible for voter registration under Regulation 13 of the Elections (Registration of Voters) Regulations, 2012 and Registration of Kenyan citizens residing out of Kenya under Regulation 34. Public agencies routinely enter into controlled data-sharing arrangements with population registration authorities for lawful service delivery, verification, and integrity purposes. Similarly, regulated private institutions such as banks, insurance firms, and telecommunications companies interface with population databases strictly for identity verification, compliance, and fraud prevention, subject to applicable laws and oversight. Therefore, the Commission has been engaging the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services on various areas of collaboration including establishing a secure Application Programming Interface (API) link with Integrated Population Registration System (IPRS) to ensure only legitimate ID and passport numbers are used. Once the engagements are complete, the Commission will inform the relevant stakeholders. Conclusion The register of voters remains exclusively under the custody and control of the Commission, as provided for under the Constitution and the Elections Act. IEBC reiterates that personal data of voters is safeguarded in strict compliance with The Constitution of Kenya; The Elections Act, 2011; The Elections (Registration of Voters) Regulations, 2012; and The Data Protection Act, 2019. The Commission calls upon all stakeholders and partners to continue supporting lawful processes aimed at strengthening the accuracy and integrity of the register of voters, which is a fundamental pillar of democratic elections. We urge stakeholders, especially the political actors, to refrain from uncorroborated, inflammatory and divisive statements that not only undermine the integrity of electoral processes, but also the independence of the Commission. IEBC remains open for any clarification on the electoral processes. ERASTUS EDUNG ETHEKON, HSC CHAIRPERSON, INDEPENDENT ELECTORAL AND BOUNDARIES COMMISSION (IEBC)

title: IEBC and LSK Strengthen Partnership to Safeguard Electoral Integrity16th Feb 2026
text: Today, the Law Society of Kenya (LSK), led by its President Faith Odhiambo, paid a courtesy call to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) . The Commission led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon welcomed the LSK delegation and underscored the importance of the engagement. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC noted that the LSK is a key institution within Kenya’s governance framework. He emphasized thatIEBC occupies a critical position in the country’s governance architecture, with a clear constitutional mandate to manage elections, referenda and boundary delimitation processes. He acknowledged the vital role LSK has played in advancing reforms in Kenya and stated that the Commission cannot effectively discharge its mandate without close collaboration with the Society. He observed that the meeting was particularly important for the new Commission as it seeks to strengthen partnerships and explore practical ways of supporting each another in delivering the respective mandates. The Chairperson further affirmed that the Commission welcomes constructive criticism. He stated that feedback that helps to improve processes, systems and the manner in which the Commission executes its public mandate is always encouraged. Addressing the LSK delegation, he reiterated the Commission’s openness to listen, learn and work together in moving the country forward. Following the by-elections, the Commission conducted a comprehensive post-election review involving stakeholders such as security agencies, political parties, candidates and civil society organizations inter alias. The review examined what worked well, identified areas that required improvement and generated lessons to inform future electoral processes. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC observed that the Commission also took note of concerns raised by stakeholders regarding the presence of gangs around polling areas, incidents of voter intimidation and harassment, electoral violence, and voter bribery. He noted that such acts are unlawful and undermine the integrity of the electoral process. While the Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee is mandated to address violations of the Electoral Code of Conduct, it can only take action upon receipt of a formal complaint. “The Commission therefore urges candidates, political parties, and members of the public to promptly report any breaches to enable appropriate action to be taken in accordance with the law, as it remains committed to ensuring peaceful, transparent, and credible elections,” he said. The Chairperson cautioned against rhetoric that undermines public confidence in the electoral body, stating: “If political leaders portray the Commission as compromised, their supporters may lose faith in the process and choose not to register or vote, believing that their participation is meaningless. We must therefore work together to support the Commission in delivering free, fair, inclusive, transparent and credible elections.” Faith Odhiambo, President of the Law Society of Kenya, expressed appreciation to the IEBC Chairperson and Commissioners for convening the meeting, noting the longstanding partnership between LSK and the Commission anchored on the rule of law and constitutionalism. She recalled that in the 2022GE, the Commission maintained an open door policy that allowed LSK to provide input on electoral laws and reforms, even under tight timelines and significant operational pressure. She reaffirmed LSK’s commitment to supporting necessary legal reforms, including campaign financing laws, to enhance the integrity and smooth conduct of elections. Odhiambo emphasized that sustained stakeholder support is essential to strengthening Kenya’s electoral processes. On judicial engagement, she called for closer collaboration between the Commission and the Judiciary to minimize last minute court orders that often disrupt electoral timelines and create uncertainty for candidates and voters. Odhiambo further proposed joint Continuing Professional Development (CPD) sessions to enhance electoral knowledge among advocates, particularly young lawyers. She underscored the importance of broader public awareness through radio, observing that while Gen Z is active on social media, a significant portion of Kenyans still rely on traditional media platforms for information. In this regard, she noted that LSK plans to conduct nationwide civic education in September and October through LSK Legal Awareness Week, including the distribution of pamphlets covering key topics to be agreed upon with the Commission. "On the issue of disinformation, we must invest significantly in media monitoring and rapid response, especially to tackle AI-generated and manipulated content that disproportionately targets female candidates. Structured engagement with digital platforms is crucial to ensure swift action against users spreading harmful content," said Odhiambo. She concluded by emphasizing the continued partnership between LSK and the Commission in areas including election observation, accreditation, and electoral reform. #26thFebByelections | #YourVoteYourFuture | #TalkwithIEBC | #StopFakeNews

title: IEBC Joins KBC in Celebrating World Radio Day, Urges Youth to Register and Participate in Elections11th Feb 2026
text: The Commission today joined KBC to celebrate World Radio Day at their HQ in Nairobi. World Radio Day is a globally recognized event aimed at celebrating radio broadcast, improve international cooperation among radio broadcasters and encourage decision-making. The Commission was represented by Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chair of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Communications, and Stakeholder Engagement Committee (VEPSEC), who delivered a keynote speech on the importance of radio in election management. In his address, Commissioner Mukhwana emphasized that radio remains the most accessible and trusted medium for reaching citizens across the country, particularly young people, marginalized communities, and those in remote areas. He noted that radio continues to play a central role in voter education, civic awareness, and the dissemination of accurate electoral information. The Commissioner used the platform to urge young Kenyans to actively participate in the electoral process by registering as voters and turning out to vote when elections are held. He observed that youth participation in voter registration remains low, despite young people constituting a significant proportion of the country’s population. “While technology continues to evolve, citizens must use the systems available today to shape their future. We should not delay participation while waiting for future innovations,” Commissioner Dr Alutalala said. He addressed concerns raised by some young people who perceive the current voting system as outdated, clarifying that electoral participation should not be hindered by the absence of mobile or phone-based voting. Drawing parallels with the evolution of radio and music technology, he noted that meaningful progress is achieved by making the best use of existing tools. Commissioner Dr Alutalala informed participants that IEBC will roll out an enhanced voter registration exercise in March across the country. The exercise will ensure services reach communities at the grassroots level. He further dismissed claims that elections can be easily manipulated, stating that the Commission has put in place robust voter identification and verification measures, including the use of national identity cards, biometric fingerprint verification, and iris recognition. “The voting procedures currently in place makes it impossible for an unregistered person to vote. The system is secure and designed to protect the integrity of the electoral process,” he said. Commissioner Dr Alutalala assured Kenyans that the 2027 General Election will be peaceful, free, fair and credible, and encouraged all eligible citizens to register and vote in order to actively participate in determining the country’s future. The Commissioner was taken through the history of radio from 1927 to the present day, highlighting key milestones and technological advancements that have transformed radio broadcasting over the years. The presentation underscored how innovations in technology have expanded radio’s reach, improved content delivery, and enhanced its continued relevance in an evolving media landscape.
