title: IEBC Holds a Prayer Breakfast Meeting with the Evangelical Alliance of Kenya (EAK)4th Feb 2026
text: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) today held a Prayer Breakfast Meeting with the Evangelical Alliance of Kenya (EAK), bringing together faith leaders and Commissioners to reflect, pray and engage on the country’s electoral journey ahead of the 2027 General Election. While addressing the gathering, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon underscored the importance of moral leadership, national unity, and collective responsibility in safeguarding Kenya’s democratic processes. He noted that the engagement with the faith community reflects the Commission’s commitment to inclusivity, dialogue, and trust-building. The Chairperson informed participants that the Commission has adopted a cycle-based approach to election preparedness, drawing lessons from the 2022 General Election and subsequent by-elections. He added that the IEBC is in the process of finalizing a comprehensive Election Operations Plan for the 2025–2027 electoral cycle, which will serve as the blueprint for planning, coordination, and execution of all electoral activities. On voter registration, the Chairperson stated that Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) commenced in September 2025 and will be complemented by Enhanced Mass Voter Registration (MVR), which is planned to be escalated to the ward level in March 2026. To support this process, the IEBC is implementing pre-registration reforms and system upgrades aimed at improving efficiency, reducing congestion at registration centres, and enhancing the overall voter experience particularly for young voters and first-time registrants. The Chairperson further noted that the Commission has invested in staff training, digitization of systems, and continuous stakeholder engagement, recognizing that election preparedness is an ongoing and inclusive process. He emphasized that preparedness does not occur in isolation, noting that the Commission continues to engage faith-based organizations, civil society, political parties, media, security agencies, and development partners. These partnerships, he said, are critical to voter education, peacebuilding, transparency, and public trust. Despite progress, the Chairperson noted several challenges facing the Commission including inadequate and delayed funding, delays in electoral legal reforms, which ideally should be finalized at least one year before a General Election to allow effective preparation. Additionally, the rising threat of misinformation and misuse of digital platforms continues to undermine public trust, peace, and social cohesion. Speaking on behalf of the faith community, EAK Chairperson Bishop Philip Kitoto noted that the Church’s mandate is to be salt in every sphere of society. He observed that Kenya, more than 50 years since independence, should not still be grappling with destructive vices, but instead should be modeling cohesion, integrity, and justice. title: IEBC Convenes Workshop to Strengthen Voter Education and Public Outreach Ahead of the 2027 General Election4th Feb 2026
text: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) is holding a workshop on the Development of Voter Education, Partnerships and Communications Performance Targets and Public Outreach Strategies for FY 2025/26/27. The workshop was officially opened by Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson, Voter Education, Partnerships, Communications and Stakeholder Engagement Committee (VEPCSE), on behalf of the Chairperson. Reflecting on Kenya’s electoral history and evolving socio-political landscape, Dr. Mukhwana emphasized that while Kenya has long been respected as a regional beacon of peace and dialogue, shifting dynamics, particularly the changing profile of young citizens, now demand new engagement strategies, deeper voter education, and stronger public trust. “The current youth demographic is unlike any previous generation. They are deeply informed, digitally connected, and politically alert. If we engage them correctly, they become our greatest asset. If we fail, they could become a powerful source of instability,” said Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana. He noted that this is why voter education is critical and emphasized the need to actively combat misinformation and disinformation. He added that there is no better way to address these challenges than by prioritising voter education, strengthening stakeholder engagement, and improving communication pathways. Dr. Alutalala further underscored the urgent need to enhance institutional credibility and reimagine public outreach, warning that weak civic education fuels confusion, mistrust, and conflict. Frankline Mukwanja, Executive Director of the Centre for Multiparty Democracy (CMD–Kenya), noted that Kenya stands at a defining democratic moment, requiring institutions to critically examine both their structural capacity and civic readiness ahead of the 2027 General Election. Drawing lessons from Kenya’s multiparty electoral history, he highlighted persistent challenges linked to institutional weaknesses, public mistrust, and inconsistent voter education, underscoring the need for accountability-driven performance targets and stronger stakeholder collaboration. Mukwanja further pointed to the changing nature of the Kenyan voter, particularly young people, describing them as highly connected, politically alert, skeptical of traditional narratives, and quick to mobilise. This generational shift, he noted, fundamentally changes how electoral institutions must communicate, build trust, and establish legitimacy. Angela Ambitho, CEO of Infotrak Research, presented the key findings from the 2024–25 research study. The study highlights that Gen Z and millennials are highly digitally connected and rely heavily on social media, while also maintaining a strong cultural identity and openness to diversity. They demonstrate active civic awareness, keen interest in current affairs and are strongly influenced by peers in decision-making. These dynamics intersect with low public trust in electoral processes, perceptions of rigging, and voter disillusionment, which negatively affect participation. The research further shows that voter education remains fragmented and often treated as a one-off exercise, focusing largely on procedural knowledge while neglecting confidence-building, transparency, grievance resolution, and visible accountability. To address these gaps, effective engagement must be tailored across demographics including youth, elderly, women, and persons with disabilities leveraging both digital and traditional media, providing clear information, and maintaining consistent institutional messaging to strengthen public trust and encourage active electoral participation. Representing URAIA Trust, Bancy Kubutha, emphasized the importance of building trust through community-driven voter education, enhancing transparency in election processes and leveraging youth networks to promote civic responsibility. She noted that structured public engagement and inclusive outreach strategies are critical to prevent misinformation, strengthen accountability and ensure peaceful participation in the upcoming elections. The workshop is out to co-create performance targets and outreach strategies aimed at strengthening voter education, partnerships and communication ahead of the 2027 General Election. #26thFebByElections #TalkwithIEBC #StopFakeNews #YourVoteYourFuture

title: Trust in election and why IEBC needs to enhance credibility in run up to 2027 GE 1113th Dec 2025
text: A month ago, Maurine Ochieng, the Commission Assistant Elections Officer (AEO) for Kisumu Central, sat in a community hall during the Citizens Election Watch forum pondering when did the wind change direction so fast. The air was thick with questions, some polite, some sharp. People spoke of “secret” biometric data, of agents barred from doing their duty, of a commission they felt was distant. But this was no protest. Officials from the IEBC sat at the front, not behind a distant podium. This was their strategy, to feel first hand, the perception gap on the Commission and its operations, years ahead of the 2027 General Election. The dialogue cut through noise with facts. • On Technology: “Is IRIS a spy tool?” A clear answer: No. It’s a legal identifier, like a fingerprint, governed by public regulations. • On Transparency: “Can agents photograph results?” Yes. Photographing Form 34A is not just allowed; it’s a safeguard. • On Integrity: “What about corruption in hiring?” The condemnation was absolute, backed by the weight of Chapter Six of the Constitution. The participants didn’t just state policies, they shared the data driving them, like the precise tally of new voter registrations in Kisumu County. Each number was a brick in a wall of credibility. From the talk, two salient recommendations were voiced. That the Commission must tell its own story.” Waiting for the final election report is too late. Continuous, proactive narrative-building is now a core part of electoral security. Secondly, the Commission must train observers adequately on the electoral process. Untrained observers, even well-meaning ones, breed misinformation. Joint training with the IEBC and other stakeholders creates a shared understanding of the process, turning watchdogs into informed partners. The Bottom Line The forum’s power wasn’t in solving every problem that day. It was in the model itself: a live, pre-emptive dialogue where the institution steps into the room, shares its workings, and listens. Trust isn’t declared after a perfect election; it is built, transaction by transaction, in rooms like that hall. The lesson for 2027 is clear: integrity is built not just by running the vote, but by openly, and early, building the trust to make it credible.

title: IEBC meets stakeholders to evaluate success of by-elections to inform conduct of electoral operations in future polls13th Dec 2025
text: The Commission Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, accompanied by Members of the Commission led a high-level Stakeholder Engagement Forum reviewing the November 27th By-Elections. The session, supported by Center for Multiparty Democracy - Kenya, brought together political parties, observers, security agencies, civil society, and the media. In his address, the Chairperson provided a clear and candid account of the electoral process. He outlined the Commission’s preparation efforts, including recruitment and training of officials, deployment of KIEMS kits, enforcement of the Electoral Code of Conduct and the management of multiple security environments across the 22 by-elections. Ethekon highlighted strong operational gains achieved under his leadership including: * polling stations opening on time, * KIEMS delivering over 99% functionality, * transparent counting and timely transmission of results, * seamless coordination with security agencies, and * effective handling of disputes and complaints. The Chairperson also addressed challenges from voter apathy and attempts to influence election officials, to logistical constraints, misinformation, and isolated security incidents in select counties. He emphasised that these issues were handled firmly and professionally, without compromising the integrity of the vote. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS, acknowledged the commitment of IEBC staff, security teams, political actors, media, observers, and community leaders whose work ensured orderly polling, timely deployment of materials, and smooth voter identification through KIEMS. “The scale of the exercise conducting the elections in the 22 electoral areas across diverse counties offered valuable insights into IEBC’s logistical systems, stakeholder engagement and field operations. This showed the critical contributions of 173 observer groups, voter educators, and the media in supporting transparency and building voter confidence,” said Marjan. The Chairperson noted that operational readiness was secured through a KSh 798 million budget allocation, which mitigated the impact of initial exchequer delays. The IEBC executed comprehensive voter education and stakeholder engagement via media channels, observers and community outreach. CMD-Kenya Executive Director, Frankline Mukwanja highlighted the core pillars of the youth activation strategy noting that Kenya’s democratic future depends on meaningful youth participation. They form the largest voting bloc but remain often disengaged or skeptical. We must bridge this gap. “Mr. Chairman, the recent by-elections were a serious test—not just for you, but for the entire electoral ecosystem. Democracy is collaborative: it relies on the Constitutional Commission, security agencies, political parties, civil society, media, and all stakeholders working together to deliver credible elections,” said Mukwanja. Kenya Editors Guild (KEG) President Zubeida Kananu called for media protection while covering electoral activities. She noted that the transparency of Kenya’s democracy is currently being paid for with the safety of media. KEG highlighted the systemic vulnerability of journalists, particularly those behind the lens during electoral activities. “Lack of prosecution has “normalized” attacks on media practitioners, treating violence against the press as an occupational hazard rather than a criminal offense. I challenge the police to move beyond internal rhetoric and activate internal mechanisms to punish officers caught on camera attacking journalists. Journalists are not just reporters; we are human beings with families. When the media is targeted, democracy is blindfolded,” said Zubeida Kananu. The Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) clarified the mandate of the National Police Service (NPS), emphasizing that their role is governed strictly by the rule of law rather than political orientation. Addressing concerns over police neutrality, the DCI maintained that officers exist solely to ensure a secure environment for IEBC officers to carry out their mandate. “The police are ready to take appropriate actions and they cannot prosecute cases based on unsubstantiated online rumours. We deal with goons as goons and criminals carry no political labels or protection from the authorities. Several suspects are already facing prosecution in court,” said Amin.

title: Commission appreciates staff for job well done in successful conduct of by-elections6th Dec 2025

title: IEBC condemns violence and disruption of voting process witnessed during byelections in Kasipul, Mbeere and Malava6th Dec 2025
text: The Commission noted with grave concern the incidents of violence, intimidation, and disruption reported in parts of the country during the 27th November, 2025 by-elections and condemned in the strongest terms possible the acts of violence, hooliganism and lawlessness experienced in some electoral areas. Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon, HSC noted that the acts of violence violated Article 81(e) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, which requires that elections be free from violence, intimidation, improper influence, or corruption and undermined the principles of Article 86 on the conduct of simple, accurate, verifiable, secure, accountable, and transparent elections. “Elections are a democratic exercise, and no individual or group has the right to compromise the peace, safety, or integrity of the process. We are working closely with security agencies to ensure swift action against any perpetrators. It is important that all political actors must uphold the principles of peaceful participation and respect for the rule of law,” said Ethekon. During the just concluded by-election, the percentage of voter turnout by each the 5 constituencies and Baring’o county was commendable. Baring’o Senate election had 25.97% voter turnout, Member of National Assembly (MNA) for Magarini (34.7%), Mbeere North (61.9%), Malava (46.26%), Ugunja (25%), Kasipul (46.4%) and Banissa (35.7%). The Chairperson urged the voters to come out in large numbers to vote noting that their vote was their voice and that participation in the polling process strengthens Kenya’s democracy and every ballot contributes to a transparent and credible outcome. The Commission also pronounced itself on misinformation that circulated claims alleging ballot stuffing in some polling stations. “These claims are false, unfounded, and intended to mislead the public. All polling stations operated under strict procedures that included the presence of agents from participating political parties, accredited observers and security personnel. Every ballot issued corresponded to a verified voter, and all processes remained open to scrutiny. “The public should always rely on official communication from the Commission and refrain from sharing unverified information that would undermine public confidence in the electoral process. The Commission remains committed to delivering a transparent, peaceful, and credible by-election. I thank all voters, officials, agents, and observers for their continued cooperation. Violence and intimidation have no place in our democracy. We call on security agencies to act firmly where breaches occur.

title: IEBC develops Strategic Communication Plan to align with new trends and enhance delivery of electoral information4th Dec 2025
text: The Commission, supported by the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA), reviewed the enhanced Strategic Communication Plan to guide the effective dissemination of electoral information, strengthen stakeholder confidence and keep pace with emerging communication trends, technologies, and lessons learned over the years. Commission Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon, HSC accompanied by fellow Commissioners during the workshop, emphasized that this strategic review reflects the Commission’s deliberate and focused steps to enhance its communication. “Developing the enhanced Strategic Communication Plan at this time is critical. With new technologies, the growing influence of digital platforms, and rising challenges such as misinformation, this revision allows the Commission to strengthen its communication with both internal and external stakeholders,” said Chairperson Ethekon. A robust communication framework will enable the Commission to address challenges before they escalate and maintain credibility, inclusivity, and a shared sense of purpose within the organization. It also aims to improve internal communication so that all staff members move forward with common understanding and unity of purpose. Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana who is the Chairperson of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Communications, and Stakeholder Engagement Committee, highlighted that the main challenge in communication is being able to harness collective experiences to determine the right moments for Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) on when? how and what to communicate. “For too long, we have relied on a enhanced Strategic Communication Plan from 2013 which is now outdated in today’s fast-evolving digital age. Persisting with this old framework would be like driving the nation’s democratic vehicle into a thick fog at Mai Mahiu with dimmed headlights,” remarked Dr. Alutalala. The Chairperson noted that from the Post-ElectionEvaluation (PEE) Report, especially the Observers’ reports, it was Communication that was picked out as an area that required improvement and in today’s fast-paced information environment, how the Commission communicate shapes how people perceive IEBC and the confidence they have in the institution. It’s not just about issuing press statements or appearing in the media — it’s about staying engaged, being transparent, and managing our reputation with consistency and honesty. That’s why strong and proactive communication is so critical in realizing our vision as a Commission. “Developing the enhanced Strategic Communication Plan couldn’t have come at a better time. With new technologies, the growing influence of digital platforms and challenges like misinformation, this review gives the Commission a chance to strengthen how it communicates to internally and externally stakeholders. A solid communication framework will not only help the Commission handle challenges before they escalate but also ensure it maintain credibility, inclusivity and a shared sense of purpose within the organization. It’s also about improving how we talk to each other internally — so that we all move in the same direction, with common understanding and unity of purpose. “By aligning our communication efforts with our core functions, we’ll improve the quality, timeliness, and impact of our messages — whether to the public, the media, or our partners. We’re not just updating a document — we’re shaping how IEBC tells its story, builds trust, and delivers on its mission to strengthen democracy in Kenya,” said Ethekon. Felix Odhiambo, the Executive Director of ELGIA, commended IEBC Commissioners on how speedy they hit the ground upon their inductions over three months ago by identifying five areas that needed immediate support being legal reforms, strategic communication, boundaries review, voter education and voter registration. “I’m happy to report that there has been remarkable progress in four out of the five areas (save for Boundaries Delimitation). Feedback received from Kenyans in our interactions and development partners is positive underlining the robust and good improvement and lets us keep up the momentum. This team will interact and enrich the draft, subject it to external validation to make it better and hopefully IEBC Plenary will adopt the enhanced Strategic Communication Plan.

This will not only enhance public trust, but also strengthen Kenya’s democracy. Further, she urged poll officials to ensure all activities are guided by the rule of law and to involve stakeholders in the relevant activities to ensure a seamless electoral process. Commissioner Ann Nderitu, Chairperson of Electoral Operations Committee, requested the participants to be committed during the training as their engagement would automatically affect how the upcoming by elections are conducted and perceived by the public. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan observed that training of poll officials remains a central pillar of quality in electoral service delivery. He also noted that during the training, attention was given to operational preparedness; pre-polling, polling and post polling activities; polling procedures, use of electronic voter identification, result management and adherence to legal and regulatory frameworks.

title: IEBC ready to conduct by-elections, reaches out to candidates to hold peaceful campaigns and meetings4th Dec 2025
text: The Commission has come out to assure the country that plans for the 29th November, 2005 By-Elections in 22 Electoral areas. Speaking while addressing the media at Anniversary towers, Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon assured the country that the forthcoming By elections will be free fair and accountable. “The IEBC has finalized key activities, including the recruitment and training of polling officials, and the deployment of logistical support teams across all electoral areas. Dispatch of election materials is ongoing and will be completed in good time for the polls” said Ethekon. Pursuant to the provisions of Article 81 of the Constitution, the Commission is required to conduct free and fair elections devoid of violence, intimidation, improper influence, or corruption. The Commission also issued a stern warning to perpetrators of violence that, the Commission will invoke the law, that gives a number of actions that can be taken by the Commission against the perpetrators of electoral violence. In a bid to address the security challenges in some of the electoral areas, the commission held a joint meeting with National Police Service and National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC)and issued a joint statement to reaffirm their joint commitment to delivering peaceful, transparent, and credible by-elections that reflect the will of the people and uphold the integrity of Kenya’s democratic institutions. Pursuant to these provisions, and informed by the prevailing security situation, the Commission in collaboration with the NPS and NCIC called upon the Political Parties and Candidates to conduct peaceful campaigns and strictly adhere to their campaign schedules and the Electoral Code of Conduct. The Commission went ahead to summon two candidates in the Kaipul by election to face the code of conduct enforcement committee on their possible involvement in security challenges being witnessed in the Constituency. Any breach SHALL attract sanctions as prescribed in the available legislative framework. The Commission Chairperson assured the nation that all critical activities for the by-elections are on course, including the recruitment and training of polling officials, the ongoing dispatch of election materials, all set to be completed ahead of polling day. Following rising political tensions and violence, particularly in Kasipul, the IEBC has intensified coordination with the National Police Service (NPS) and the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC), issuing a joint statement to assure Kenyans of robust security arrangements to guarantee the integrity of the upcoming elections. Violence. IEBC has condemned electoral violence and warned it will take stern action, including campaign suspensions and issuing summons to enforce the Electoral Code of Conduct. This week, two candidates from Kasipul constituency were summoned to appear before the Commission’s code of conduct enforcement committee to answer for their possible involvement in violent incidents. Any breach of the code will attract strict sanctions as prescribed by law. The Commission urges all political parties and candidates to run peaceful campaigns, adhere to officially scheduled campaign times, and strictly follow the Electoral Code of Conduct. The chairman encouraged Voters to turn out in large numbers and elect leaders of their choice in the By- election areas. The chairperson reiterated the Commission’s resolve to uphold Kenya’s constitutional mandate and guaranteed a free, fair, and peaceful elections.

title: IEBC and Public Service Commission meet to review human resource instruments4th Dec 2025
text: The Commission, with the support from the State Department for Public Service and Human Capital Development, held a workshop to review its human resource instruments. A multi-Directorate Technical Working Committee, comprising a technical team from the Commission has been tasked with reviewing the IEBC organisation structure, career progression guidelines, salary structure and the Human Resource manual and policy. This is aligned with the initiative by the National Treasury to integrate the Human Resource Information System (HRIS) with the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) and other statutory systems, to enhance efficiency, accuracy, and accountability in managing human resource and financial data across government systems.

title: IEBC joins inter agency forum on data sharing framework to support Continuous Voter Registration exercise11th Nov 2025
text: The Commission participated in an interagency meeting to explore Data Sharing framework strategies that will support the ongoing Voter Registration (CVR) exercise. The team seeks to develop a collaborative framework and draft a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the IEBC and the State Department of Immigration and Citizen Services for secure and lawful data sharing. This should cover access to data on national Identity Cards and Passports, Integrated Population Registration System (IPRS), Records of deceased persons and other relevant datasets for the purpose of updating the Register of Voters. The IEBC team was led by Director Electoral Operations Moses Sunkuli, Director Legal Services (DLS) Chrispine Owiye and Director Information Communication Technology (DICT) Michael Ouma. Speaking during the event, Sunkuli reiterated that the CVR exercise is a vital step in ensuring that every eligible Kenyan has the opportunity to participate in shaping the country’s future through democratic elections. The exercise is particularly directed towards young people who have recently attained 18 years, and all citizens who have not yet registered or need to update their voter information. NRB Secretary Dr Chrstopher Wanjau and team leader said the bureau targets to register over 6.7 million Kenyans by 2027. “We produce National Identity Cards every day and it would be ideal for the IEBC staff to seize the opportunity and have close proximity to the youth, who visit our Bureau offices to collect IDs, to register them straight away,” said Wanjau. The Bureau also confirmed that thousands of ID cards that have not been collected from their offices and sought collaboration and teamwork to whip up citizens to collect them. The meeting agreed to form join secretariat to actualize an API to IPRS Integrated Population Registration System that will come in handy in the pre-registration module.

title: Commission highlights strategies to empower women in politics during mental health and inclusion forum11th Nov 2025
text: The Commission joined the Centre for Multiparty Democracy Kenya (CMD-Kenya), in partnership with Six Political parties to a round table discussion to explore the intersection between political participation, emotional wellbeing and gender inclusion. The forum themed “A Mental Health Approach to Women’s Political Participation” was held on 29th October 2025, at Kingfisher Nest Hotel in Nairobi and it brought together participants from CMD-Kenya, IEBC, Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP) and select political parties. Joyce Ekuam, the Ag. Director of Voter Education, Partnership and Communications, representing the Commission Secretary and CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, explored IEBC sustained efforts to enhance women’s participation in politics. The presentation addressed the legal provisions on special interest groups, the IEBC’s constitutional and institutional mandate and the persistent challenges Kenyan women face in seeking elective positions. IEBC highlighted the legal framework that governs elections in Kenya and emphasized the initiatives to promote women’s leadership through voter education, stakeholder engagement and inclusive electoral processes. It also touched on the Commission’s constitutional mandate to support special interest groups. Ekuam further addressed the persistent challenges Kenyan women face in seeking elective office. Specifically, the Commission has made deliberate efforts to intervene and promote women participation in elections including development and implementation of a dedicated Gender and Social Inclusion Policy, reduced nomination fees for women candidates and enforcement of the two-thirds gender rule by rejecting non-compliant party lists. In addition, the Commission has established Women, Youth and Disability Inclusion Coordination Committees to enhance women participation in elections. Other interventions implemented include deploying an Electoral Risk Mapping Tool to identify and mitigate gender-based and cyber violence against women and strict enforcement of the Electoral Code of Conduct to penalize political malpractice. Beyond policy, the IEBC works to make electoral processes practically inclusive. This involves accrediting women-led organizations as voter educators and observers, granting priority voting to expectant mothers and using gender-sensitive messaging in voter education campaigns. “Partnerships with organizations like FIDA-Kenya strengthen these efforts, supported by vibrant IEBC Communication Centres to monitor and respond to electoral gender-based violence. The Commission also has a gender-sensitive budget policy to ensures funds are allocated for these critical initiatives,” said Ekuam. The presentation also recognized financial mechanisms that support women’s leadership, such as the Women Enterprise Fund, the National Government Affirmative Action Fund (NGAAF) and the Political Parties Fund. In conclusion Ekuam emphasized the need for continued action by identifying inclusion gaps, promoting mentorship, building candidate capacity and upholding the two-thirds gender rule in all government appointments. CMD-Kenya reiterated that empowering women in politics must include strategies to protect their mental wellbeing. “Participants reaffirmed commitment to foster a political culture grounded in empathy, inclusivity and mental wellness, ensuring that women are not only present in leadership but are also supported holistically,” said CMD-Kenya.

title: IEBC undertakes capacity building for Commissioners to enhance understanding of polling process ahead of by-elections11th Nov 2025
text: The Commission undertook capacity building for Chairperson, Vice Chairperson and members of the Commission on electoral processes in a special workshop hosted in Mombasa.. The capacity building session, organized by the Directorate of Electoral Operations through the Electoral Training Departmen, was meant to enlighten the Commissioners to diligently deliver on IEBC Constitutional mandate, one of them being the forthcoming 24 by-elections set to be conducted on 27th November 2025 across the country. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan emphasised the importance of Commissioners understanding the electoral process.. “We’re now delving into the mechanics of our work: how elections and referenda are conducted, how voter registration is managed, how technology enhances these processes and how all these elements combine to ensure credible elections.”. Commissioner Anne Nderitu, CBS who is the Chairperson of the Electoral Operations Committee, encouraged the trainees to carefully interrogate the presentations as it is the backbone of election management. She emphasized that the Commission has a rich knowledge base to deliver the tailored content.. During the closing ceremony, the Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon, HSC expressed satisfaction with the Commission’s internal trainers. He encouraged the CEO to institutionalize a knowledge management centre to facilitate ongoing knowledge transfer and experience sharing within the Commission.. Further, the Chairperson urged the Commission to expand training to external stakeholders in the electoral sector, ensuring they remain well-informed and actively engaged with the electoral sub-system.. The customised training was designed to equip the Commissioners with hands-on knowledge and experience in electoral-legal framework, voter registration, conduct of elections, results management, election technology, stakeholder engagement, communication among others. These initiatives underscore the Commission’s dedication to enhance public trust and strengthen Kenya’s democracy.

title: Commission engages State Department for Diaspora Affairs, explores ways to enhance voting for citizens living outside Kenya11th Nov 2025
text: The Commission’s Technical Working Group (TWG) on Diaspora Voter Registration and Elections on Monday 3rd November, 2025 held its inaugural session in collaboration with the State Department for Diaspora Affairs (SDDA). The meeting marked the official launch of the TWG’s engagements and outlined its mandate aimed at enhancing the participation of Kenyans living abroad in the electoral processes. The meeting, which was chaired by Commissioner Ann Nderitu, CBS Chairperson of Electoral Operations Committee, discussed the Terms of Reference (TORs) guiding the TWG. She noted that the TWG will review the legal and policy framework governing diaspora voting, assess existing participation measures, develop mechanisms to improve electoral inclusion, and address logistical, legal, and administrative challenges associated with diaspora voter registration and elections. Commissioner Nderitu emphasized that the TWG will operate autonomously, with minimal involvement from Commissioners. “The role of Commissioners and the Chair will remain minimal. The TWG will carry out the technical work and present its recommendations to the Commission for policy consideration,” she clarified. Reflecting on past diaspora voter registration initiatives, Commissioner Ann noted that despite significant financial investment, the outcomes remained limited. She challenged the team to focus on innovation, efficiency, and value for money. “We need to find better, smarter ways to ensure that Kenyans abroad are effectively registered and able to vote, without incurring unsustainable costs,” she said. The State Department for Diaspora Affairs team was led by Mr. Edwin Limo, Director of Liaison and Partnerships. He reaffirmed the Department’s commitment to working with the Commission to ensure eligible Kenyans abroad are registered and able to vote as required by the Constitution.

title: IEBC engages Bunge la Mwananchi to sensitise members to support ongoing Continuous Voter Registration exercise6th Nov 2025
text: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission IEBC) led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, interacted with the grassroots voice of the people, Bunge La Mwananchi, in a meeting under the theme “Your Participation is not an Option, it is Your Patriotic Duty!” The Commission praised the crucial civic work of Bunge La Mwananchi (The People’s Parliament), acknowledging their presence across 36 counties and their call for youth to register and participate in democratic processes. The Vice Chairperson Fahima observed that challenge is ringing across the Republic: “You have waited long enough... I urge you to come out in large numbers to fulfill your constitutional mandate.”“Your ID is not a card. Its your POWER!”, she implored. The Bunge La Mwananchi Chairman, voiced his concern on the low registration especially by the youth and pledged to collaborate and implore them to register. IEBC committed to free, fair and credible elections, while Bunge La Mwananchi was ready to partner with the Commission through an MoU for mobilization.

title: Commission conducts staff sensitisation on Information Security Management System6th Nov 2025
text: Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, conducted a two-day sensitization workshop on Information Security Management System (ISMS) and ICT Policy in Naivasha. The workshop is both timely and essential to strengthen the Commission’s technological backbone, enhance information security posture, and align operations with best practices in digital governance. Ms. Fahima observed that as the Commission reflects on the heart of its mission information security is no longer just an ICT issue; it is an organizational culture. “This workshop is not just another item on our calendar. It is a moment to pause, reflect and act. Let us evaluate how we handle information, how we safeguard it and how we can improve the systems that power every function of the Commission,” Ms Fahima observed. Ms. Fahima made a clarion call to all members of staff to ensure that the policy: Strengthens the Commission’s technological backbone and aligns operations with digital governance best practices, Recognizes that every staff member plays a role in protecting the integrity of our data, Moves beyond maintenance to innovation — driving creativity and continuous improvement, and Usestechnology to build a modern, trusted and technology driven electoral institution. “As stewards of democracy, our commitment to robust ICT policies and a strong ISMS framework is non-negotiable. When we secure our technology, we secure the will of the people,’’ she emphasized. The Chairperson, Research, Innovation, Information & Communication Technology Committee, Prof. Francis W. O. Aduol, called upon members of staff to embrace innovation as a key enabler of excellence in elections management. He emphasized that innovation must be embedded in how the Commission secures, manages and delivers electoral processes. He urged staff to think beyond routine operations and adopt creative technology-driven solutions that enhance efficiency, transparency, and data protection throughout the electoral cycle. “By promoting a culture of curiosity, collaboration and continuous improvement, the Commission can strengthen its digital infrastructure and uphold the integrity of elections,” noted Prof. Aduol. The Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS, reiterated that information security demands more than compliance checklists, it calls for a collective mindset shift. “This journey is not about ticking compliance boxes. It is about strengthening our institutional backbone — building a Commission that is secure by design, not just by chance. The stakes have never been higher. The credibility of our elections — and the trust of citizens — depend on our vigilance,” said Marjan

title: Ethiopian Civil Society Organisations for Elections tours IEBC, studies strategies to promote womens participation in polls6th Nov 2025
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, hosted a delegation from the Coalition of Ethiopian Civil Society Organizations for Elections (CECOE) under the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) who are in the country for a study visit on strategies the Commission deploys to promote women’s participation in the electoral processes. The Vice Chairperson noted that even though Kenya has made progress in enhancing inclusion, participation of women in the electoral process is still a matter of concern, as they remain underrepresented. “There is need for targeted interventions to attain minimum requirements of gender equity to promote political representation,” she said. The Commission has put in place supportive legal and institutional structures, but women still face challenges in attaining equal participation and representation in Kenya due to societal contextual/cultural, religious factors, formal and informal rules and norms/gender roles. The Commission has made significant strides towards promoting the political participation of women, not only as voters, but also as candidates through development and implementation of a gender and social inclusion policy, cut down to half the nomination fees for women compared to other categories, rejected Party nomination lists that are not compliant with two-third gender rule. Further, the Commission has a Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee to hear, determine, and penalize candidates and political parties that perpetrate electoral malpractice: violence, intimidation, discrimination and destruction of campaign materials and gender rule. The Vice Chairperson said the Commission has also established Women Coordination Committees (WCC) that has national and grass-root levels which bring together women-led and women serving organizations from across the country to supplement the Commission’s outreach and advocacy efforts. This is besides deploying an Electoral Risk Mapping tool to enable identification of early signs of electoral violence including gender-based violence, cyber violence against women and girls. Abera Hailemariam, the Executive Director CECOE, said that the delegation seeks to strengthen the knowledge, skills, and strategies used by Kenya to advance women’s political participation. The mission will also promote regional peer learning and networking to encourage cross-country collaboration and exchange of innovative approaches.

title: IEBC meets Amnesty International, discusses integrity and protection of human rights in electoral process27th Oct 2025
text: The Commission hosted a delegation from the Amnesty International led by its Executive Director, Irungu Houghton. The meeting discussed possible areas of collaboration including promotion of electoral integrity, protection of human rights and enhancement of voter participation in electoral processes. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon assured the delegation that the Commission is strengthening electoral integrity through key initiatives including internal reforms, legal reviews and stakeholder engagements. On his part, the Amnesty International Executive Director, Hughton Irungu, committed to support and work closely with the Commission, especially in the areas of human rights protection and public participation in electoral processes.

title: IEBC engages National Chamber of Commerce to promote awareness and youth participation in electoral process27th Oct 2025
text: The Commission held a collaborative meeting with representatives from the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI). The stakeholder engagement aimed to deepen mutual understanding and explore areas for partnership in strengthening the electoral processes. IEBC Chairperson, Erastus Ethekon, HSC, highlighted that the Commission is working closely with relevant stakeholders to review and enhance the electoral legal framework, with the goal of establishing a stronger and more credible electoral system for Kenya. “IEBC is eager to partner with KNCCI to promote electoral awareness, encourage youth participation, and support a stable business environment,” said Ethekon. He encouraged KNCCI to use its extensive network to motivate eligible voters to register and actively participate in the upcoming electoral processes. KNCCI President Dr. Erick Rutto pledged the Chamber’s full support. It was agreed that the two institutions have a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that will guide collaboration and strengthen their ties.

title: Commission pays tribute to former Prime Minister Raila Odinga as he takes final bow out of Kenyas political landscape27th Oct 2025
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) bows its head in deep sorrow and solemn respect at the passing of His Excellency, The Rt. Hon. Raila Amolo Odinga - a statesman of rare courage, patriot of unmatched devotion, and steadfast architect of Kenya’s democracy. The Chairperson, Members and Staff of the Commission extend their heartfelt condolences to the Odinga family, and to a nation united in grief. Kenya has lost a towering son whose voice, vision, and valour shaped its destiny. The Rt. Hon. Odinga’s indomitable spirit guided our nation through its most defining moments - from the struggle for multiparty democracy, to the birth of the 2010 Constitution; and relentless quest for credible, transparent and people-centered elections. His sacrifices strengthened the institutions that uphold the sovereign will of the Kenyan people. Indeed, his life is etched in our democratic foundations - in every reform, every freedom and every ballot cast. For this, we owe him a debt of eternal gratitude. In his honour, the IEBC rededicates itself to his vision - to defend integrity, impartiality, and transparency in every election, and to ensure that the voice of every Kenyan remains sacred and supreme. Go well, Great Son of Kenya. Your dream for a just, democratic and united nation will forever inspire our path.

title: Commission visits Mashuuru Primary Boarding School, engages students and gives back to community in CSR gesture20th Oct 2025
text: As part of its ongoing Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives, the Commission organized a community outreach activity at Mashuuru Boarding Primary School in Kajiado County during the launch of the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise held on 29th September 2025. The school, being one of the polling stations used by the Commission, was selected to benefit from this initiative in recognition of its long-standing partnership with the IEBC in facilitating electoral activities. The CSR activity was led by the Deputy Commission Secretary – Operations, Ruth Kulundu, and the Deputy Commission Secretary – Support Services, Obadiah Keitany. The event aimed to give back to the community, promote education, and strengthen the Commission’s relationship with local residents. During the activity, the Commission donated various essential items to the school, including stationery to enhance learning, sanitary towels to promote menstrual hygiene and support girls’ education, footballs to encourage cocurricular activities, and school bags to motivate pupils and foster community development. In addition, the IEBC team planted 20 trees within the school compound as part of its commitment to environmental conservation and sustainability. The tree-planting exercise symbolized the Commission’s dedication to nurturing not only democracy but also a greener, healthier future for communities across the country. Through this CSR initiative, the Commission demonstrated its commitment to education, youth empowerment, and community development.

title: IEBC joins Canadian High Commission, engages young innovators on use of emerging technology in electoral process20th Oct 2025
text: The Commission joined the Canadian High Commission to participate in a Gen-Z Innovators discourse on future deployment of election technology in Kenya. The meeting, which was convened by Mr. Kimani Mungai, Senior International Assistance Officer at the Canadian High Commission provided a platform for young Kenyans to demonstrate innovations and mastery of emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence, blockchain and digital systems and how these technologies can enhance transparency, efficiency and accountability in electoral processes. The IEBC Chairperson, in his remarks, commended the Canadian High Commission for providing platforms that bridge innovation, youth and democratic governance. He emphasized that Kenya must continue to “push the frontiers of innovation” as it prepares for future elections, adding that the Commission welcomes ideas that strengthen the constitutional principles of impartiality, neutrality, efficiency and transparency in election management. He further noted that while technology must operate within the legal framework, IEBC remains open to exploring reforms and collaborations that will allow for the safe and lawful adoption of new systems. The Chairperson lauded the youthful presenters for their optimism, courage and advocacy, urging them to continue influencing change through innovation and dialogue. The meeting highlighted the importance of multistakeholder collaboration between innovators, development partners and public institutions in shaping the next phase of electoral transformation in Kenya. “If we can trust technology to move our money safely, surely we can trust it to move our democracy forward,” the Chairperson remarked. Speaking at the session, Commissioner Prof. Francis Aduol, Chairperson, Research, Innovation, Information and Communication Technology Committee, commended the young innovators for their patriotism and creativity. “When young minds and visionary leadership meet, innovation happens. The future of democracy is digital — and it must be inclusive.” He emphasized that progress happens when generations collaborate and that trust remains the foundation of every election. “As a Commission, we believe in opening our doors to new ideas that redefine how citizens connect with democracy — today, tomorrow, and beyond 2050,” he said. The engagement underscored IEBC’s commitment to empowering youth voices, nurturing partnerships and promoting innovation that builds a transparent, technology-driven electoral process where every vote counts and every voice is heard. The IEBC continues to engage partners and young innovators in strengthening democracy through technology and inclusive participation. The meeting was also attended by senior management team led by Ruth Kulundu, DCSOperations, DEO, DICT, DLS and Ag. DVEP&C.

title: Commission clears 181 candidates to contest in 24 by-elections in November20th Oct 2025
text: The Commission finalised the registration of 181 candidates to contest in the 24 electoral areas with by-elections scheduled for 27th November 2025. Following this, a 10-day window, has been opened for resolving any disputes arising from the candidate registration process. “The commission deployed a monitoring and reporting tool for use during the registration exercise that was meant to solicit ground information for our future improvements,” said Gideon Balang, Manager Electoral Operations. Out of the 24 electoral area, Nairobi County’s Kariobandi North County Assembly Ward within Embakasi North Constituency and Chewani ward in Galole Constituency of Tana River County have the highest number of nominees cleared being 16. Tembelio ward in Moiben Constituency in Uashin Gishu County has only one candidate. “Candidates are commencing campaigns upon successful registration by the respective Returning Officers. The campaigns shall end on Monday 24th November 2025, being 48 hours before the by-election day. The campaign time shall run daily from 7.00a.m. to 6.00p.m. during the campaign period,” added Balang. The Commission urged all candidates and the public to maintain peace and order during the campaign period. “Candidates are urged to strictly adhere to the Code of Conduct during the electioneering period,” said Balang.
