This year’s elections was however different as the institution introduced use of an online voting platform, dropping the reliance on physical ballot papers and bulky ballot boxes. This initiative was developed and designed by the schools’ ICT department. The Commission offered technical and professional guidance. The elective positions contested for include President CSs for sports, ICT, education and environmental affairs. Other position ere governor for Grade (1 – 9) and MP for each stream in every grade. The voters roll had 1,263 voters with 26 polling stations. Leonard Njenga, the Senior Elections Officer (SEO) for Dagoretti North Constituency served as the returning officer. He started off by holding a planning meeting with Riara Primary & Junior school elections committee at the IEBC Dagorretti North Constituency office, where an MoU was signed between the Commission and the school. “We agreed that the school uses its manual register to verify voters. This determined the voter turnout. The Commission thus provided a returning officer, a presiding officer, a DPO and Five clerks while Riara Primary & Junior School nominated its teaching staff to serve to check and confirm students register,” said Mr. Njenga. The school also provided computers installed with voting software while the Commission provided election materials, which included ballot boxes, polling booths, seals, indelible inks, pens and IEBC branding materials to help simulate the traditional polling station for the pupils to experience the manual elections. After poll results trickled in, Maya Maina was elected President with Kemunto Nyaribo (education), Omar Mathenge (ICT), Adelina Muthoni (environmental studies) and Mascuid Adenelected CS Sports. In total the election recorded a 100 percent turnout and there were 72 elective positions and three polling centers – Riara primary and Junior school annex 1, Annex 2 and Annex 3.

title: IEBC meets UoNs Department of Geospatial and Space Technology, explore areas for collaboration15th Apr 2025
text: The Commission met with the Department of Geospatial and Space Technology, University of Nairobi, who had paid a courtesy call. The purpose of the meeting was to explore collaboration opportunities, particularly in areas of electoral mapping and research. The meeting which was chaired by Deputy Commission Secretary for Operations, Ruth Kulundu, proposed a number areas of collaboration, including joint research, policy reviews and analysis. Additionally, the parties explored the development of electoral tactile maps, which would enable individuals with visual impairments to access and utilize them effectively.

title: Music Copyright Society seeks Commission expertise to conduct elections of directors8th Apr 2025
text: Music Copyright Society of Kenya Limited (MCSK) on Thursday paid a courtesy call on the Commission and discussed areas of mutual interest and collaboration. Led by MCSK Chief Executive Officer Dr. Ezekiel Mutua, MBS the team was welcomed by Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, who pledged to work closely with the Society. MCSK Governing Council intends to conduct elections of its directors to fill vacancies in the regions being Rift Valley (one) and Nairobi (two – author and publisher). “The reason for our visit to IEBC is to request the Commission to assist MCSK in the conduct of these elections by providing materials and technical staff to oversee the polls,” said Mutua. The Society has a total membership of 15,728 spread across seven regions in the country — Nairobi, Central, Eastern and North Eastern, Coast, Nyanza, Western and Rift Valley. MCSK asked the Commission to provide support material being two technical officers per each region to oversee the election, ballot boxes in the two regions that will be conducting elections and any other material that IEBC would recommend to make the election free, fair, transparent and verifiable. Director Voter Registration and Election Operations (DVREO) Moses Sunkuli in response said the Commission demanded that MCSK should comply with IEBC regulations for conducting external election by submitting MSCK constitution on their election, provide Governing Council resolution sanctioning the election and appointing IEBC to preside their elections. Further, the Commission asked MCSK to submit their general rules on organization of election, number of elective positions being contested, MCSK Code of Conduct, if any and the Register of Voters eligible to participate in the election. “All these requirements are mandatory and must be presented at inaugural meeting,” said Gedeon Balang, Manager Election Operations.

title: IEBC and diaspora technical working group discuss strategies for 2027 Diaspora Voting8th Apr 2025
text: The Commission Secretary/CEO, Marjan H. Marjan, MBS led a team from the IEBC in an online meeting with the Diaspora Technical Working Group (DTWG) to address the key issue of diaspora voting for the upcoming 2027 general elections. The DTWG, a volunteer-driven initiative, plays a pivotal role in advocating for the electoral rights of Kenyans residing abroad. Through their work, they strive to ensure that Kenyans in the diaspora can meaningfully contribute to the country’s democratic processes. The DTWG is a diverse and inclusive body representing Kenyan communities from around the world, with membership spanning across Africa, Asia, Oceania, Europe, North and South America, and the Middle East. The group brings together professionals from various fields, including legal experts, educators, technologists, business leaders, and community organizers. At its core, the DTWG emphasizes the importance of enhancing the role of the diaspora in national governance and electoral matters, with particular focus on marginalized groups such as youth, women, and persons with disabilities. The meeting was attended by 34 members of the DTWG from countries such as China, the United Kingdom, France, Finland, Australia, Germany, Rwanda, the UAE, Switzerland, and Norway. During the discussions, Martin Koyabe, chair of the DTWG, underscored the need for increasing diaspora voter participation, which had been low in the previous elections due to several factors, including a limited number of polling stations, restrictive IEBC criteria, and the high costs associated with voting. In response to these challenges, Koyabe proposed expanding polling locations beyond Kenyan embassies, making voter registration more accessible through biometric systems, enhancing civic education, and exploring digital solutions to reduce costs. He also emphasized the importance of collaboration with the IEBC to push for legal reforms that would ensure the diaspora’s full constitutional right to vote. Dr. Kenny Karanja, a member of the DTWG, highlighted the geographical challenges faced by voters in the Americas, particularly in the United States and Canada, where vast distances present logistical difficulties. He proposed adding additional polling stations, based on population distribution and convenience, in key areas such as the US and Canada, and also mentioned the potential for expanding polling stations in other countries with significant Kenyan populations, such as Brazil. In his response, Marjan addressed the legal, logistical, and financial hurdles surrounding diaspora voting. One of the main concerns raised by the CEO was the legal restriction that currently limits polling stations to locations within Kenyan embassies and high commissions. This constraint, he pointed out, made it difficult to establish temporary polling stations in other areas. Additionally, Marjan expressed concerns about the time zone differences, particularly in countries such as Australia, and questioned whether the diaspora’s proposals took these challenges into account. jan also emphasized the importance of accurate population data to support effective planning for diaspora voting. He noted that while general population estimates exist, there is a need for more precise data to guide decisions on the number of polling stations and the allocation of resources. Furthermore, Marjan highlighted the budgetary constraints facing the IEBC, stressing the need for cost-effective solutions to address the fiscal challenges the country is currently experiencing. The CEO called for a collaborative approach between the IEBC and the diaspora to address these issues and improve the overall electoral process. He emphasized that elections should be viewed as an investment in the country’s democratic future and that partnerships between the government and the diaspora would be crucial in overcoming the logistical challenges. Marjan also acknowledged the role of technology in improving voter registration and education, while reminding participants of the legal requirement for biometric data in the process. In conclusion, Marjan’s underscored the need for clear legislative proposals, accurate data, and a unified approach to ensure that diaspora voting becomes both feasible and effective. The importance of collaboration, innovative solutions, and strategic planning was emphasized as key components in achieving a successful diaspora voting system in the 2027 elections. In attendance from IEBC during the meeting were CPA Obadiah Keitany, DCS-Support Services; Ruth Kulundu, DCS-Operations; Chrisphine Owiye, OGW Director of Legal Services; Khadija Ramadhan, Ag. Director of Supply Chain Management; Purity Njeru, MCPA; and Abdi, Manager of Voter Registration.

title: ICT team holds workshop, discuss ways to strengthen election technology for 2027GE8th Apr 2025
text: IEBC with support from the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (Elgia Afric) held a five-day workshop in Nairobi to discuss the 2027 Election Roadmap. This workshop aimed to assess and improve election technology by incorporating key lessons learnt from previous General Elections and insights highlighted by election observer reports and audits, which are instrumental in refining electoral systems for greater efficiency and transparency. Michael Ouma, HSC, Director Information Communication and Technology, emphasized the need for the roadmap to align with the Strategic Plan, to ensure that technological advancements are seamlessly integrated into the electoral process. He highlighted the increasing influence of new media and Artificial Intelligence (AI), noting that while they offer opportunities, they also present challenges that must be proactively addressed. He observed there was need to adapt to these changes and implement secure and efficient solutions to strengthen the electoral system. Deputy Commission Secretary – Support Services, CPA Obadiah Keitany, MBS, said it was important to continuously improve technology in elections. “The Commission has come a long way in integrating technology into its electoral processes, particularly in results transmission. In the 2022 General Election, IEBC successfully leveraged electoral technology to transmit the presidential election results. However, the Commission must use this opportunity to refine its systems and strive to serve Kenyans better in the future,” he said. Boniface Mc Olwal, ELGIA Programme Manager, representing Executive Director Felix Odhiambo Owuor, underscored ELGIA’s strong commitment to supporting the Commission in strengthening its electoral processes. He underscored the importance of clearly defining the role of election technology in election management, particularly in its use by the Commission, political campaigns and in electoral dispute resolution. He observed that the roadmap must provide a clear direction on whether election technology is merely an enabler of trust or synonymous with trust itself. The IEBC Commission Secretary/CEO, CPA Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS, commended staff for their dedication and hard work in successfully delivering the 2022 General Election. He urged staff to stay ahead of the game as technology continues to evolve and reaffirmed the Commission’s commitment to strengthening Kenya’s democratic processes through technological advancements and innovations. Referencing Section 44 of the Elections Act, 2011, he reiterated that election technology must be simple, verifiable, secure, accountable and transparent—principles embedded in Kenya Integrated Election Management System. As the Commission reflects on past lessons and prepares for 2027, he highlighted the crucial role of technology in modern electoral management. He concluded by emphasizing that the workshop is a continuation of an inclusive and thoughtful conversation on leveraging technology to uphold the democratic aspirations of the Kenyan people.

title: IEBC revises training content for Commissioners induction course and set by-elections timelines session-class8th Apr 2025
text: The Commission, with support from the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA), is conducting a four-day workshop on Development of Training Content and Methodology, and By-elections timelines. Recognising the complexity of elections and the need for specialised expertise, the Commission is developing a training programme for newly recruited Commissioners. This programme will equip them with essential knowledge for policy formulation, strategic planning, and effective oversight. Continuous training programmes will also ensure that Commission staff remain updated with the latest electoral best practices. Additionally, following the 2022 General Election, 17 electoral area vacancies have arisen due to election petitions, resignations and the passing of elected leaders. To address these vacancies and uphold democratic governance, the Commission has developed a draft By-Election Operational Plan. While opening the workshop, Moses Sunkuli, Director of Voter Registration & Electoral Operations, emphasised the urgency of detailed by-election planning, given that some vacancies have exceeded the 90-day timeline due to the absence of a Commission. “We are moving beyond basic orientation to comprehensive training that equips Commissioners with a strong understanding of electoral processes, ensuring they lead with confidence and competence,” stated Sunkuli. Representing ELGIA CEO Felix Odhiambo Odwuor, Bon MakOlwal, Senior Manager of Electoral Reforms, reinforced the need for the Commission to take ownership of the induction process to fully prepare new Commissioners for their responsibilities. “This workshop is crucial in developing a structured curriculum that will equip the new Commissioners to oversee elections effectively, especially with pending by-elections,” added MakOlwal.

title: IEBC submits on Budget Policy Statement to Senates Finance and Budget Committee25th Mar 2025
text: The Commission appeared before the Finance and Budget Committee of the Senate to submit views on the 2025 Budget Policy Statement. The Budget Policy Statement outlines Commission's key priority areas and budgetary needs for three fiscal years from the Financial Years (FY) 2025/2026 to 2027/2028. Commission Secretary/CEO, Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS while addressing the Committee members emphasised the need for adequate funding of the Commission to enable it deliver on its mandate. Marjan highlighted the importance of funding key electoral activities such as conduct of the General Election, election technology, voter registration, voter education, boundary delimitation, by-elections, pending bills and legal reforms among others.

title: Commission legal technical committee holds workshop to streamline the election timelines14th Mar 2025
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) Legal Technical Committee, with support from the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA), held a two-day workshop from March 3rd to 4th, 2025, in Upperhill, Nairobi to streamline election timelines as part of ongoing legal reform. After the 2022 General Election, IEBC actively engaged in legal reforms guided by insights from the post-election evaluation report, launched on January 16, 2023. As a result, the legal reform process has led to the development of several Bills and amendments to statutory instruments, some of which are currently at various stages of consideration before Parliament. One of the key legislative proposals, the Elections (Amendment) Bill, 2024, was adopted by the Senate on December 5, 2024. It was subsequently transmitted to the National Assembly on February 12, 2025, where it was referred to the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee (JLAC) for deliberation and public engagement. In line with this, JLAC invited stakeholders and the public to submit their comments on the Bill by March 5, 2025. The Commission is now tasked with reviewing the Bill to assess its impact on election processes and timelines. Additionally, the IEBC is analyzing the election timelines from the 2022 General Election to propose necessary adjustments in preparation for the 2027 General Election. These efforts will enable the Commission to submit a well-informed memorandum to the National Assembly, contributing to Kenya’s broader commitment to democratic governance and electoral transparency. By actively participating in this legislative process, the IEBC aims to ensure that electoral laws are responsive to emerging challenges and aligned with best practices. The workshop’s outcomes will play a critical role in shaping the Commission’s recommendations on the Elections (Amendment) Bill, 2024, reinforcing its mandate to oversee free, fair, and credible elections in Kenya.

title: Commission feted for promoting inclusivity in electoral process during 7th DIAR Awards13th Mar 2025
text: The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) was one of the major winners during the 7th National Diversity and Inclusion Awards & Recognition (DIAR) gala, held on Friday, 7th March 2025, at the Sarit Expo Centre in Nairobi. The Commission scooped the Best Constitutional Commission and Independent Office award on Ethnic Representation, which feted its dedication to fostering inclusivity and diversity in Kenya’s governance and electoral processes. Further, the IEBC was named the runner-up in three other key categories: Best Constitutional Commission and Independent Office on representation for Persons with Disabilities (PWD), Best Constitutional Commission and Independent Office on Equitable Allocation of Opportunities and Resources and Best Constitutional Commission and Independent Office in propagating Good Governance, Transparency, and Accountability. These four awards highlight the Commission’s continuous efforts in ensuring fair representation of marginalized groups in the electoral process. Acting Director of Voter Education and Partnerships Amina Soud, HSC was present to receive the wards. The DIAR Awards, celebrate individuals and organizations championing environmental, social and governance principles alongside diversity, equity, inclusion and belonging values in Kenya. This year’s gala theme was, “Awarding Investors in People, Planet Guardians and Champions of Prosperity for Posterity,” which emphasized the importance of inclusivity, sustainability and social change. The award gala was organized by Daima Trust, a social enterprise established in 2017, which actively promotes diversity and inclusion through various initiatives, including the DIAR Awards and workshops. IEBC in the 2022 General Elections demonstrated a firm commitment to fostering an inclusive electoral process by implementing policies and initiatives that ensure marginalized groups actively participate in governance. Article 100 of the Kenyan Constitution mandates Parliament to enact legislation that promotes the representation of marginalized groups, including women, youth, persons with disabilities, ethnic minorities, and marginalized communities. In alignment with this, IEBC expanded its definition of special interest groups to include Kenyans living abroad, the elderly, prisoners, students and street families, ensuring their voices are heard in electoral matters. To enhance participation, IEBC follows an electoral-cycle approach, incorporating inclusivity across the pre-election, election and post-election phases. During the pre-election period, the Commission focuses on gender and youth-inclusive budgeting, advocating for adherence to the two-thirds gender rule, and conducting targeted voter registration. In the election phase, initiatives such as reduced nomination fees for youth candidates, peace campaigns, and inclusive voting measures help ensure fair participation. Post-election activities involve conducting audits on youth representation, proposing youth-responsive legal reforms, and developing inclusive voter education strategies. IEBC also developed a Gender and Social Inclusion Policy (GSIP), 2019 to provide a framework for increasing the participation of Special Interest Groups in electoral processes. The guiding principles of this policy include equity, gender equality, non-discrimination, human rights adherence, transparency, and accountability. The GSIP mandates the IEBC to adhere to the Two-Thirds Gender Principle and ensure at least 5% of appointive bodies comprise persons with disabilities. It also emphasizes the importance of making election offices and events accessible, reserving at least 30% of all procurement opportunities for women, youth and persons with disabilities. The Commission is also proposing legislation to protect marginalized groups in boundary delimitation. Additionally, the Commission utilizes inclusive technology for voter registration and ensures voter education materials are available in accessible formats, including braille, sign language interpretation and audio materials. To institutionalize inclusivity, the Commission has established Women Coordinating Committee (WCC), Youth Coordinating Committee (YCC) and Disability Inclusion Coordinating Committee (DICC) across all 47 counties. It has also accredited organizations that serve and are led by special interest groups as election observers and voter education providers. Furthermore, the Commission has deployed Kenyan Sign Language (KSL) interpreters in IEBC events and broadcasts, partnered with Signs Media to use the AssistAll App for accessible electoral information and conducted accessibility audits to ensure polling stations are user-friendly for persons with disabilities. Additional efforts include setting up Communication Centers in every constituency to engage youth and women in electoral discussions and collaborating with key agencies like the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) and the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) to enforce electoral integrity and security. Despite these efforts, IEBC faces significant challenges in ensuring full inclusion of marginalized groups. Limited funding restricts the Commission’s ability to implement extensive voter outreach programs. Voter apathy among marginalized groups also remains a challenge, as does the lack of political goodwill in fully implementing the two-thirds gender rule. Additionally, cultural beliefs in some communities continue to hinder the participation of women, youth, and persons with disabilities in electoral processes. The IEBC’s recognition at the DIAR Awards 2025 underscores its unwavering commitment to fostering a diverse and inclusive electoral environment. Through policies, programs, and collaborations, the Commission is paving the way for fair representation and greater participation of marginalized groups in Kenya’s governance. However, to achieve full inclusivity, efforts should be made to address funding gaps, political resistance and societal barriers. As Kenya progresses toward more democratic and inclusive elections, the IEBC remains a key driver in ensuring that every citizen, regardless of background, has a voice in shaping the nation’s future.

title: IEBC budgets Sh61.7 billion to conduct 2027 General Election funded in three fiscal years13th Mar 2025
text: The Commission, led by Deputy Commission Secretary - Support Services Obadiah Keitany, MBS who represented the Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS appeared before the National Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Departmental Committee (JLAC) to consider the 2025 Budget Policy Statement. The budget plan, which is worth Ksh 55 billion funded by the National Treasury, serves as a baseline assumption to be used in the preparation of the 2027 General Election. The budget also shows that the Commission has an overall deficit of Ksh 6.7 billion, with pending bills standing at Ksh 3.827 billion. “The Commission would like the General Election to be funded over the three Financial Years starting with the 2025/2026 to cater for pre-election activities worth Ksh15.3 billion. The 2026/27 year, the Commission has budgeted for Ksh 25.4 billion while the 2027/28 it has Ksh 21 Billion. The total budget stands at Ksh61.74 billion,” said Keitany. The Commission projects to register additional 5.7 million new voters, majority being youth who have attained the age of majority. In preparation of the 2027 General Election, the Commission projects to gazette 55,393 polling stations up from 46,229 in 2022 and procure Kenya Integrated Election Management System (KIEMS) kits worth Ksh 7 billion to replace the 45,352 currently in use that were bought in 2017. Only the 14,000 KIEMS kits purchased in 2022 will be retained. “The KIEMS have been used for 10 years and can be formatted and donated to another government institution for use. Technology has changed fast and we can rely on them now,” Keitany told the Committee. Keitany noted that the Commission would like the General Election budget to be funded over the three Financial Years starting from 2025/26 to cater for pre-election activities like voter registration and acquisition of the election technology software and hardware. The DCS also informed the Committee that the Commission is expected to conduct by-elections upon the reconstitution of the Commission and will request separately for resources to conduct the exercise. Currently, there are 14 vacant positions being Senator (1), Member of National Assembly (4) and Member of County Assembly Ward (9).

title: Young Parliamentarians pay courtesy call to IEBC, discuss youth participation in elections13th Mar 2025
text: A delegation from the Kenya Young Parliamentarians Association (KYPA) today paid a courtesy call to the Commission to discuss IEBC mandate, achievements, partnerships and areas of mutual interest. KYPA delegation was led Chairperson Hon Gitonga Mukunji, MP Manyatta Constituency, and was welcomed by Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS. The Young Parliamentarians sought information on what the Commission is doing to increase youth participation in electoral process. Specifically, the delegation was keen on the strategies used by the Commission to increase voter turnout in elections, enhance voter registration among the youth and areas within the legal framework that need to be amended to promote youth participation in elections. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, underscored the role the youth play in strengthening Kenya’s democracy noting that the Register of Voters in the 2022 General Election had over 40% youth. “The Commission, ahead of the 2022 General Election, constituted the Youth Coordinating Committee (YCC), a conglomeration of youth-led and youth-serving organisations that worked with the Commission in voter education and mobilization. YCC with support from the Commission mobilized youth to register as voters in colleges and universities, and trained voter educators in 49 universities countrywide,” said Marjan. The Commission also implemented deliberate strategies to reach out to the youth by partnering with social media corporations like Meta (Facebook) and X (Twitter) to tackle misinformation and disinformation and directed online traffic to its website for information. The Commission is also actively engaging the youth on online social media platforms like X_Space (formerly Twitter Space) to inform and educate them on various issues on the electoral process. Marjan urged the youth to come out and register as voters once the Commission opens the Continuous Voter Registration exercise. Kenya Young Parliamentarians Association Chairperson Hon. Gitonga Mukunji said that to enhance youth registration, they will utilise the multisectoral approach and reach out to Ministry of Interior and National Administration @InteriorKE to ensure young people who attain age of maturity are issued with identity cards and subsequently register as voters. “Kenya Young Parliamentarians Association will also onboard young leadership in Parliament in voter education to enable them know the electoral process and push to have the Commission funded in time to conduct its activities throughout the election cycle. KYPA targets to increase the voter turnout at the 2027 General Election from 64% attained in 2022GE to over 80% because young people’s voice count,” said Mukunji.

title: IEBC takes part in People Dialogue Festival, commits to have inclusion in electoral process13th Mar 2025
text: The Commission took part in panel discussions across various thematic “Villages” and set up an exhibition stand, primarily manned by young staff members, during this year’s People Dialogue Festival (PDF) held from 5th to 8th March, 2025 at Uhuru Park, Nairobi. Led by Deputy Commission Secretary (DCS) Operations Ruth Kulundu, IEBC reaffirmed its commitment to transparency, voter education and ensuring inclusivity in Kenya’s electoral processes. The festival, an initiative by the Centre for Multiparty Democracy (CMD-Kenya), plays a crucial role in fostering democratic dialogue and empowering citizens to shape Kenya’s political future. The DCS also participated in a panel discussion at the Political Dialogue Village alongside representatives from the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP), the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA) and the Promoting Inclusive Electoral Reforms in Kenya (PIER-K) Consortium. The discussion centred on strategies employed to enhance inclusive electoral reforms in Kenya. Additionally, Edgar Aswani the Acting Senior Communication Liaison Officer, joined a panel discussion at the Youth Village to address barriers to accessing electoral services and the need for increased youth participation in the electoral process. This annual event themed "Building a Collaborative Democracy for Kenya’s Sustainable Future" brought together leaders, members of the public, government institutions, civil society organizations and the private sector stakeholders to discuss pressing societal challenges, foster citizen participation and co-create solutions for Kenya’s sustainable development. Many young attendees, who engaged with the IEBC team, sought answers to key electoral questions including the commencement date of voter registration, the appointment of new IEBC commissioners, the timeline for boundary delimitation, the process for recalling Members of Parliament and the scheduling of pending by-elections. Beyond answering questions, the IEBC team also conducted voter education, emphasizing the importance of democracy and the Commission’s role in safeguarding electoral integrity in Kenya. The stand was managed by Benjamin Kimwei, Voter Education Coordinator; Edgar Aswani, Acting Senior Communication Liaison Officer; Margaret Muinde, Assistant Elections Officer for Dagoretti North Constituency; Alicia Kioni, an intern in the Department of Communication and Public Affairs; and Daniel Mathenge. Their collective efforts helped inform and engage citizens on democratic responsibilities.

title: South Sudan Electoral Commission receives valuable lesson in election plan, management26th Feb 2025
text: The South Sudan National Election Commission (NEC) called on the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) for a week-long benchmarking tour and peer exchange forum. The delegation arrived on Monday, February 17th to Friday, February 21st, 2025, at the Kenya School of Government, Lower Kabete Campus. The workshop was openned by Felix Koskei, the Head of Public Service and Chief of Staff. In his opening remarks, Mr. Koskei underscored the exciting opportunity for knowledge exchange between IEBC and South Sudan's NEC creates. He stressed the importance of both entities learning from each other, given the constantly evolving political and technological landscapes that impact election management. Welcoming the South Sudanese delegation, IEBC Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan emphasised the mutual and cordial relationship between the two sister election management bodies. He noted that this is the first Electoral Commission hosted by the IEBC in 2025 and reassured participants that the program's design is comprehensive and meticulous. According to Marjan, all topics were carefully selected, and facilitators were well-prepared to ensure that both Electoral Management Bodies (EMBs) gain invaluable lessons for future implementation. Prof. Abednegom Akok, Chairperson of South Sudan's NEC, expressed his gratitude to the Kenyan Government, the Kenya School of Government, and the IEBC for their hospitality and willingness to host the delegation and share their invaluable knowledge and experiences. He urged delegation members to remain attentive and fully engaged throughout the workshop. Throughout the week, the delegation explored various thematic areas, including the electoral-legal framework, which forms the cornerstone of election management. They delved into the evolution of voter registration and the innovative strategies deployed in Kenya since independence. Additionally, the delegation was enlightened on the crucial role of technology in enhancing voter registration, candidate registration, voter identification, election results transmission, and the accreditation of various election stakeholders. A key takeaway was the understanding that while electoral technology is vital, its credibility must be built on the right foundation being the right specifications, proper training, deployment, and stakeholder engagement. The South Sudan delegation also toured the IEBC Headquarters, the Commission warehouse, and the IEBC county office in Kiambu, to appreciate the devolved offices for efficient and seamless management of elections at different levels. Participants were awarded certificates after successfully completing the week-long learning tour.

title: IEBC engages stakeholders in EU Electoral Follow-up Mission to strengthen elections26th Feb 2025
text: IEBC Led by Deputy Commission Secretary – Operations Ruth Kulundu, participated in a roundtable discussion organised by the European Union (EU) Electoral Follow-up Mission to Kenya. The forum, which was at Sankara Hotel in Nairobi, offered a platform for key electoral stakeholders to provide feedback and recommendations aimed at strengthening Kenya’s electoral processes. Members of the EU Electoral Follow-up Mission and other stakeholders engaged constructively with the IEBC team, sharing insights on challenges and opportunities for improving electoral integrity and inclusivity. Speaking at the forum, DCS Kulundu reaffirmed the Commission’s commitment to upholding free, fair, and credible elections. “Engaging with stakeholders is essential in ensuring that our electoral processes are inclusive and transparent. We welcome these recommendations and will consider them as we continue to refine our electoral framework,” said Kulundu. Stakeholders present included political parties, representatives of Persons with Disabilities, women and youth groups, the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC), the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), the Media Council of Kenya, the National Council of Churches of Kenya among others. Each group shared perspectives on enhancing electoral accessibility, transparency and fairness.

title: Commission hosts Office of Controler of Budget to benchmark on IPSAS accounting26th Feb 2025
text: The Commission hosted a delegation from the Office of the Controller of Budget (OCOB) for a benchmarking exercise on the implementation of the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) Accrual basis of accounting. The OCOB delegation, led by CPA Pamela Okatch, Chief Manager Finance and Accounts, was welcomed by the Deputy Commission Secretary - Support Services, CPA Obadiah Keitany. Keitany assured the delegation that the Commission will provide any technical support needed in their transition journey. Director Finance CPA Osman Ibrahim said the Commission adopted the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) accrual basis in the 2011/2012 financial year and is among the few state agencies that have fully implemented this standard of accounting. This makes IEBC a reference point for best practices in IPSAS accrual accounting. Accountants CPA Patrick Nyakira and CPA Clifford Rono were at hand to showcase the Commission’s IPSAS accrual journey, benefits gained, milestones achieved, key lessons learnt, challenges and made recommendations of how best an organization can implement the standard to ensure smooth transition from IPSAS Cash to IPSAS Accrual basis. The discussions also covered key areas including reporting on current assets and liabilities, inventories, applicable accounting policies, accrual of revenues and expenditure, contingent assets and liabilities and gratuities. CPA Pamela Okatch lauded the Commission’s commitment to financial integrity. “This has been an enlightening experience. Your team’s dedication is commendable and we look forward to further collaboration,” said Okatch. The benchmarking session reinforced the Commission’s leadership in public sector financial reporting and strengthened the mutual collaboration with OCOB in advancing best practices in accounting.

title: Management reviews draft Strategic Plan, to be used in development of 2027 EOP18th Feb 2025
text: The Commission, with support from the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA), held a workshop for Senior Management to review the draft IEBC Strategic Plan 2024 -2029. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS noted that the previous plan (2020-2024) enabled the Commission to conduct a successful 2022 General Election. “The Commission operates in polarized political environment and we should be responsive to the emerging issues. The Commission’s Strategic Plan must be dynamic and respond to environmental and technological changes. We are here as a team to learn from the past and address the future. The Commission needs to continuously strengthen itself and respond to the gaps identified in its operations,” said Marjan. Marjan thanked ELGIA and IFES together with development partners including European Union, UKAid, USAID and UNDP for supporting the development of the draft plan. Bon Makolwal, ELGIA Senior Manager Electoral Reforms, who represented Chief Executive Felix Odhiambo Odwuor, noted that the Strategic Plan will inform areas of strategic support and collaboration with the Commission. This is a step in the right direction as incoming Commissioners will find a draft ready for their review. Deputy Commission Secretary (DCS)- Operations Ruth Kulundu noted that the draft strategic plan is a result of extensive work done by the Technical Working Group and aligns with the Commission’s goals. “As Management, I call upon each one of us to analyze their areas to ensure that every aspect of the election cycle is captured as we head towards the conduct of the 2027 General Election. It is important to note that from this Strategic Plan the Commission will develop the Elections Operation Plan (EOP) for the 2027 General Election. The draft Strategic Plan will also be subjected to stakeholder engagements.

title: Data protection now legal right, obligation for data controllers and data processors18th Feb 2025
text: Article 28 – Right to have human dignity respected and protected. Article 31 – Right to privacy (person/home/property; information relating to family or private affairs unnecessarily required/revealed; privacy of communication). Article 35 - Right to access of information (including right to correction or deletion of untrue or misleading information that affects that person). The Data Protection Act, 2019 (the Act) which came into force on 25th November, 2019 established the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) with the aim of regulating the processing of personal data. The Act also provided for: registration of data controllers and data processors with the regulators; the principles and obligations of personal data protection; grounds for processing of sensitive personal data; transfer of personal data outside Kenya; exemptions from the provisions of the Act; and enforcement of the Act, including penalties and breaches. Consequently, various regulations have been developed to guide the application and enforcement of the Act. These include: Data protection (General) Regulations, 2021; data protection (Registration of Data Controllers and Data Processors) regulations, 2021; Data protection (Complaints Handling and Enforcement Procedures) Regulations, 2021; Registration Regulations, 2020; and Registration of persons (National Integrated Identity Management System) rules, 2020. Several guidelines have also been developed to guide engagement and communication with data subjects, including ‘Guidance notes for Electoral Purposes’. IEBC (The Commission) has developed a draft policy framework for data privacy and protection whose objective is to provide a guideline on collection, processing, storage, usage, security and disposal of personal data collected and that is controlled/processed by the Commission. In addition, the Commission has registered with the ODPC as both a data controller and a data processor in compliance with the Act. Data is the oxygen that fuels every organization. As the data becomes more accessible and efficient through various innovations, the progress comes with a price of vulnerability of the same personal data. The arising risks to data privacy rights are real and the consequences can be devastating. Therefore, the need to protect personal data has never been more urgent than now. The laws in place have set very high standards for handling personal data. As a Commission, we must build a strong data protection culture for long-term compliance and security of the massive personal data in the Commission’s control. Send your comments to dpo@iebc.or.ke, Agatha Wahome Ag. DREB&RM / Data Protection Officer (DPO)

title: Commission submits to National Assembly s JLAC on Constitutional Amendment Bills18th Feb 2025
text: The Commission submitted proposals of the Constitution of Kenya (Amendment) Bills before the National Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee (JLAC) on January 22, 2025. Led by Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan the team submitted the Bills, which seek to amend the Constitution by entrenching in it the National Government Constituencies Decentralised Fund (NGCDF), the Senate Oversight Fund, the National Government Affirmative Action Fund and the Economic Stimulus and Empowerment Fund. Marjan noted that the Commission appreciates the concerns raised in the Bills. However, the Commission suggested a review of the proposals as reflected in the matrix presented to JLAC. The meeting was chaired by Honourable George Murugara (Tharaka), with Hon. Mutuse Ekomas Mwengi serving as the Vice Chairperson, along with 13 committee members. “The Commission has endeavored to highlight its submissions in matrix format on the relevant provisions of law proposed for amendment, clause of the Bill, comments on the same and proposals for review where necessary. The Commission requests the Committee (JLAC) to consider the issues identified and urge the honourable House to consider the said proposals,” said Marjan. The NGCDF seeks to facilitate grassroots development projects at the constituency level, the Senate Oversight Fund will empower the Senate in fulfilling its oversight role, the National Government Affirmative Action Fund will support affirmative action initiatives targeting marginalized groups and the Economic Stimulus and Empowerment Fund aims to promote economic empowerment for women, youth, and persons with disabilities. These amendments raise critical concerns regarding their constitutional validity and potential implications on governance structures. The proposed amendments could result in the national government encroaching upon functions that constitutionally belong to county governments. Existing funds have functioned effectively for over a decade without constitutional entrenchment, suggesting that the issue is administrative rather than legal. The Commission advocates for a review of existing legislative mechanisms to ensure effective service delivery without undermining constitutional principles The recommendations were presented to the National Assembly’s JLAC by Director of Legal Services Chrisphine Owiye, OGW, alongside legal pupil Geoffrey Daudi on behalf of the Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS.

title: EU Electoral Follow-up Mission pays courtesy call to IEBC, discuss Election Observer report18th Feb 2025
text: The Commission hosted the European Union Delegation Electoral Follow-Up Mission to Kenya that was led by Dimitra Ioannou, Electoral Expert and Team Leader and accompanied by Coln Fahy, a Legal Expert. The mission aimed to assess the Commission's electoral process that it deployed in the conduct of a successful 2022 General Election. It also purposed to review the implementation of recommendations proposed in a report of the EU Election Observation Mission. The report evaluated the regulatory framework to affirm if the constitutional provisions on gender equality are fully implemented and how the Commission enforced legislation on campaign finance. The EU mission also called for improvements in election technology and called for the Commission to be provided with timely funding to implement continuous voter education. The delegation was received by the Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, EBS. The CEO expressed his gratitude for the support accorded to the Commission by the EU and acknowledged that the recommendations proposed will improve the electoral process. The CEO highlighted the Commission's progress in implementing the recommendations in its processes, including legal reforms on the 2/3rd gender rule. The visit is part of the Commission's stakeholder engagement meetings ahead of the 2027 General Election. The discussion focused on the implementation of the recommendations and the gaps identified. In attendance were Deputy Commission Secretary-Operations Ruth Kulundu, Deputy Commission Secretary-Support Services Obadiah Keitany, and representatives from various directorates.

title: IEBC oversees conduct of Garissa University Students Council polls in Garissa Township17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission oversaw the conduct of the Garissa University Students Council Elections (GaUSO) held on 23rd November 2024. The institution, which is within Waberi ward of the Garissa Township Constituency, reached out to the Commission to manage the process of their students elections. Prior to the conduct of election, Noor Gedi the Senior Elections Officer for Fafi Constituency, who served as the Returning Officer, took the initiative to take the students and tutors through voter education to learn the tenets of democracy and why it is important to vote into office responsible leadership. “The Commission held a series of meetings with the University Electoral Commission to plan on the requirements for a smooth election and advised on the number of personnel and material required,” said Gedi. Reaching out to the students is part of the broader responsibility by the Commission to inculcate democratic tenets among the youth at an early age. The Garissa University student population is over 5,000 and hold their student council elections every academic year. The University has its own established electoral commission comprising of lectures and students body representative as per the GaUSO Constitution. It is guided by the GaUSO Constitution, students’ rules and regulations and the Kenyan Constitution. The University electoral commission was mandated to carry out the nomination, vetting of candidates as well as monitor campaigns. On the Election day, the students (voters) were identified by use of nominal roll as register where the name of the voter was crossed using a red pen and after voting the index finger was marked with an indelible ink. The Garissa University Students’ Organisation (GaUso) Election is done in two phases. The first phase has the election of 12 delegates. The elected delegates then vote to office seven officials being Student Council President and a deputy, a secretary general, academic, finance, welfare and sports directors. These seven positions were voted into office unopposed. Compiled by Abdi Yunis- Ag. CEM Garissa County and Noor Gedi - SEO, FAFI Constituency

title: Commission develops data inventory and conducts data protection impact assessment17th Feb 2025
text: Kenya enacted the Data Protection Act, 2019 on 25th November, 2019 making it a primary statute on data protection in the country and as such each state agency was required to incorporate mechanisms to strengthen and support this new law. To integrate this law in its operation, the Commission, which acts as a Data Controller and Data Processor, held a workshop to develop the IEBC Data Inventory and conducted a Data Protection Impact Assessment. The workshop held in Nairobi ran from 9-11 December, 2024. This is part of the awareness campaign being incorporated by the Commission for data safety. The implementation of the Data Protection Act is geared towards safeguarding personal information in an increasingly digital world. Indeed, the Commission holds huge personal data of over 22 million registered voters besides the other categories of data in its possession being candidates, temporary election officials, employees, litigants, election observers, venders, media personnel, political party agents and petitioners. Some of the sensitive data that is controlled or processed at IEBC include health, children, biometrics, ethnicity/racial information, wealth information, sexuality. Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, in a speech read on his behalf by Director ICT Mike Ouma, noted that unauthorized access or breach of such data can lead to dire consequences not only for the Commission but also for the data subjects. “The Commission has a mandatory responsibility to protect the personal information in its possession,” said Marjan. Ouma on his part said in the build up to the 2027 General Election, the Commission must operate careful so as not to share Personal Identifying Information (PII) with Political parties. “During the next election, we will have a high interest in the PII and with the advent of Artificial Information (AI), such data must be protected and only shared out to responsible agencies,” said Ouma. Marjan underpinned the need for the Commission to build a data protection culture as a long-term compliance and security of data collected and processed in the entire electoral cycle. He challenged the workshop participants to propose quick wins and recommendations that would ensure the Commission builds a strong data protection culture, complies with relevant data protection laws and raises the bar of protecting the massive personal data that it holds.

title: Commission engages stakeholders in regional conference on use of AI, social media in polls17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission took part in a two-day regional conference on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), digital and social media in elections in Kenya. The conference was organized by Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA) with support from United States Agency for International Development (USAID-Kenya) and UKAid brought together leaders, experts and practitioners to explore how technology is shaping the future of democracy and elections in Kenya and across Africa. Felix Odhiambo, Executive Director at ELGIA, noted that the recent decision by Africa Union (AU) to adopt guidance to harness artificial intelligence to meet Africa's development is the best step in the right direction. However, he pointed out that it brings with it opportunities and challenges in use of AI in election management and requested for a strong legal framework to ensure ethical use of AI tools. The resolutions and recommendations passed from the conference will provide important input in the conversation on use of AI, digital and social media in the electoral process. IEBC Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS noted that AI, digital and social media are three of the greatest innovations to have widely, rapidly and seamlessly influenced the globe. Africa and the world at large lives in a new era that demands new strategies, new thinking and new leadership. “The application of AI will define the future, and therefore Africa must develop new capabilities, new tools and new regulatory frameworks to ensure that AI works for it, for its partners, for its interests, and for its values, and not against it,” observed Marjan. Wiper Political Party Leader, Kalonzo Musyoka, noted that ahead of 2027 General Election, technology will be important to guide the campaigns, voter education and voter registration. AI is changing the way things are done and has the capacity to change people. This reality must be borne in mind for those in election management. Eliud Owalo, the Deputy Chief of Staff in the Executive Office of the President, who represented Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said that AI is crucial in elections as it will reduce the number of election petitions by increasing the accuracy of election outcomes and it has the ability to produce tailor made messages targeting individual voters informed by preferences and demographics leading to personalized voter outreach. “Further AI can be used in resource allocation, improve data management, storage and analysis of electoral data and enhance timeliness to allow real time decision making, thus reducing human error and reinforcing public trust in the electoral process. AI can also be used to monitor public opinion by analyzing conversations and trends on social media,” said Owalo. Marjan noted that recently, the Commission used its X-platform (formerly Twitter Space) to engage the public, especially the youth, in understanding its mandate and answering questions. The Commission has also established its presence on social media platforms such as Facebook, X (Twitter), Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, Tik Tok and LinkedIn. Forbes Advisor, in 2023, placed the number of social media users worldwide at 4.9 billion people and it’s expected that this number will increase to about 5.85 billion users by 2027. Further, the CEO in recognition of the opportunities presented by AI and the number of voters that can be reached on social media, noted that Election Management Bodies (EMBs) across Africa have cautiously embraced the use of AI, digital and social media in electoral activities including integrating AI into election management to improve the accuracy and fairness of elections, while preventing fraud. AI systems like interactive chatbots and fact-checking tools are empowering citizens and marginalized groups to influence policy discussions, ensure respect for human rights, and hold governments to account. AI tools can detect and counter the spread of fake news, deep fakes and bots, that mostly thrive on digital and social media thus ensuring a more informed and less manipulated electorate. Further, AI can be used to fight hate speech in heterogeneous settings by identifying the banned terminologies within the shortest time. Though there is considerable confidence and traction to adopt AI, digital and social media in electoral administration, these platforms may have potential risks that can ruin the gains made by many EMBs in Africa and so the need for necessary cautions when planning to introduce them.

title: IEBC engages technical working groups to enhance collaboration and diaspora voting17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission's senior management met with the technical working group of Kenyans in Diaspora on November 20, 2024, to discuss enhancing collaboration and addressing issues related to their democratic rights. IEBC made a presentation on election management in Kenya and provided statistics on the participation of Kenyans living in the diaspora in the 2022 General Election. The Diaspora technical working group expressed concern over the limited number of registration and polling stations, especially in vast countries like the United States of America, which has only three. The team was assured that the participation of Kenyan citizens living outside the country is a provision of the law, which is being realized progressively.

title: Commission seeks to build consensus on Election Campaign Financing law17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission participated in a multisectoral workshop aimed at building consensus on Election Campaign Financing. The workshop was hosted by the Electoral Law and Governance Institute of Africa (ELGIA). Participating institutions included Parliament, IEBC, the Financial Reporting Centre, EACC, DCI, KRA, CBK, academia, key civil society organizations, and leaders representing various sectors of society./p> The key objectives of the workshop were to: Evaluate the implementation status of Election Campaign Financing legislation. Conduct a comparative analysis of international best practices. Contextualize Kenya’s constitutional, legislative, and policy framework on election campaign financing. Build consensus on election campaign financing reforms. Present comparative perspectives from other jurisdictions. Strengthen stakeholder collaboration for effective reform In his opening remarks, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS, noted that the Commission faced challenges in operationalizing and enforcing election campaign financing laws, largely due to a lack of political goodwill to enact the necessary legislation. Mr. Marjan highlighted the significance of the judgment rendered in the consolidated Constitutional Petitions No. E540 of 2021 and No. E546 of 2021, filed by Transparency International, Katiba Institute, Africog, and Philip Gichane. The petitions sought judicial intervention to give effect to the implementation of election campaign financing regulations. He further elaborated that, pursuant to this judgment and with support from development partners, the Commission has: Reviewed the Election Campaign Financing Act and generated an Election Campaign Financing (Amendment) Bill, 2024, Revised the Election Campaign Financing Regulations, 2024 and Identified strategies to address the limits on contributions and expenditures. Mr. Marjan called on participants, particularly election stakeholders, to sustain the push for regulating election campaign financing, emphasizing its necessity as a constitutional requirement. Additionally, the Acting Manager for Legal Reforms, Political Parties, and Campaign Financing, Ruth Makuthu, presented the current status of the Election Campaign Financing law, highlighting issues, challenges, and recommendations for improvement. At the conclusion of the workshop, it was agreed that the consultant would compile the proposals and submit a comprehensive report for further deliberation by the participating institutions.

title: IEBC attends technical meeting to discuss and consolidate critical reforms ahead of 2027 GE session-class17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission participated in a technical workshop from 23rd to 26th October, 2024 hosted by the Elections Observation Group (ELOG) in Machakos County. The workshop drew participants from members of Civil Society Organizations' technical working group on elections and electoral duty bearers which discussed and consolidated critical electoral reforms advocated by different duty bearers. The Commission was represented by Ruth Makuthu, the Ag. Manager Legal Reforms, Political Parties and Campaign Financing. The meeting received updates on the reforms by different institutions and consolidated proposed critical reform areas in the run-up to the 2027 General Election. The team developed a draft matrix aimed at tracking the implementation of recommended reforms as a CSO tool to lobby and advocate for the implementation of the agreed minimum reforms ahead of the 2027 General Election. The joint resolutions by the technical team will be shared with the participating institutions before engagement with election stakeholders.

title: Commission provides polling booths to help Botswana conduct special voting in Nairobi17th Feb 2025
text: Botswana High Commissioner to Kenya, Andrew Sesinyi, paid a courtesy call to IEBC and was welcomed by Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS. Botswana will hold its General Election on 30 October 2024 to determine the composition of its 13th Parliament as well as local councils across the country. Botswana has selected Kenya among the foreign nations to conduct special voting for its citizens living abroad at their High Commission offices in Nairobi on 19th October. Botswana High Commissioner to Kenya requested IEBC to provide polling booths to be used during the elections. Marjan pledged to support Botswana in conduct of its election.

title: IEBC develops 3-year MTEF budget to guide operation through to 2027 General Election17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission led by the Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan H. Marjan, MBS held a workshop to develop its Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) for the Financial Years 2025/2026, 2026/2027/ and 2027/2028. The Commission prioritizes prudent financial planning, expenditure and accountability to guarantee value for money while improving service delivery. While opening the workshop, Marjan observed that Government policies and plans affect the mandate of the Commission in various ways, especially through budget cuts meant to finance new priority areas. “The biggest lesson we should learn from the current state of affairs is that we must be smart in our budgeting processes by properly selecting programmes and aligning them with the Strategic Plan and Commission’s mandate in what we can call “the irreducible minimums”. This approach will give us a form of ring-fenced assurance of guaranteed funding as well as shield the Commission budget from targeted cuts,” he added. The workshop brought together Senior Management and County Elections Managers.

title: Nigerian delegation tours IEBC, benchmarks on poll management and women inclusion17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission hosted a delegation from the National Assembly of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and discussed issues related to election management and its impact on women’s political representation. The delegation is being supported by the National Institute for Legislative and Democratic Studies (NILDS) in collaboration with the United Nations Women (UN Women) to benchmark in various countries and learn best practices in promoting gender responsive legal/constitution reforms. The delegates were informed that some of the strides the Commission has made in promoting women participation in elections in Kenya include: halving of payable fees for registration of women candidates, establishment of women coordinating committees across the country as well as rolling out the gender and inclusion policy. The Commission Secretary/CEO, Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS observed that in order to make significant strides towards promoting women's political participation, an Electoral Management Body needs to take the electoral-cycle approach that looks at women participation in pre-election, election and post-election phases.

title: Commission launches initial process to guide development of the Strategic Plan 2024-202917th Feb 2025
text: The Commission, with support from the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES) held a workshop in Machakos to assess its 2020-2024 Strategic Plan, which will inform the development of the 2024-2029 Strategic Plan. Commission Secretary/CEO, Marjan H. Marjan, MBS said it was important to have a Strategic Plan which is a roadmap that will guide the Commission accomplish its desired goals. The development of the current Strategic Plan was pegged on the Vision 2030, Mid-Term Expenditure Framework Plans and Big Four Agenda. The new Strategic Plan will be based on the same but hinged on current government policy that is the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA). “The implementation of the Strategic Plan is not a straight line journey. It has to go through ups and downs and must be prepare with an understanding of the past and current challenges and how to chat the path for the future. This has to be done with an understanding of the internal and external environmental risks, some of which the Commission can’t control but affect performance, like the absence of Commissioners to formulate policy and oversight, Said Marjan. The Deputy Commission Secretary (DCS) – Support Services, Obadiah Keitany, MBS noted that the assessment of the 2020-2024 Strategic Plan is critical and participants have been given the responsibility to come up with what worked, what didn’t work and the level of implementation of the plan. The 2020-2024 Strategic Plan is anchored on six Key Result Areas (KRAs): strengthening corporate governance, strengthening legal framework, effective conduct of the elections, enhanced public outreach, equitable representation and strengthening strategic operations of the Commission. Marjan noted that the 2024-2029 Strategic Plan should enable the Commission to invest in a resilient culture in a polarized political environment by cultivating trust among various stakeholders through public participation, ease of access to information and enhanced participation in the boundaries and election processes. IFES carried out an assessment of current Strategic Plan based on the Commission’s review and proposed several recommendations for consideration in drafting of a new Strategic Plan, which included cutting down of the KRA and sharpening them to align them with our priorities and modern challenges for greater focus in conduct of boundaries delimitation, 2027 General Election and nurturing a culture of trust and positivity among our stakeholders.

title: Hordes of students, public visit iconic IEBC booth at the Nairobi International Trade Fair17th Feb 2025
text: The IEBC stand continues to attract huge interest from members of the public, dignitaries and students seeking electoral related information. The Commission is participating in the 2024 Agricultural Society of Kenya’s Nairobi International Trade Fair (NITF) at the Jamhuri showground from 23rd to 29th September 2024. This year’s theme is 'Promoting Climate Smart Agriculture & Trade Initiatives for Sustainable Economic Growth'. The Show provides an opportunity to learn more about the electoral processes and activities, and interact with various electoral equipment and materials. IEBC stand was been awarded the best Independent Commission Stand after competing against other Constitution Commissions at the Show.

title: IRI and CMD seek to strengthen inclusivity of marginalised groups in the electoral process17th Feb 2025
text: The International Republican Institute (IRI) and the Centre for Multiparty Democracy (CMD) on 16th September, 2024 paid a courtesy call to the Commission in a meeting that sought to strengthen the inclusion of marginalised groups in Kenya's political process. The meeting also marked an important step towards building a more inclusive and equitable political future for all and emphasized the need for continued collaboration, identify and support Commission strategies to promote marginalised groups to make meaningful participation in Kenya's electoral processes. Specifically, the meeting highlighted the importance of addressing challenges in party nomination lists, which are left at the discretion of political parties, as well as the issue of underrepresentation of persons with disabilities (PWDs) in county governments. Other issues that were discussed include how to simplify the voting process, access to polling stations for PWDs and provision of braille ballot papers. IRI and CMD outlined strategies to enhance political participation and representation of marginalised groups and ensure there are adequately represented in party nomination processes. The two organisations committed to working closely with political parties and IEBC stakeholders to create frameworks that address the unique challenges faced by these groups. IRI and CMD have conducted series of strategic sessions focused on empowering members of marginalised groups, particularly women, youth, and persons with disabilities, within the country's major political parties. The political parties include the United Democratic Alliance (UDA), Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), Wiper, FORD Kenya, and Amani National Congress (ANC). During these multi-party strategy sessions, participants from the five political parties discussed the challenges faced by marginalised groups to have inclusion in party nomination lists. They called for the Commission to eliminate the barriers that hinder equal representation and ensure the marginalised groups are represented and heard in decision-making platforms. The Commission expressed its support for the initiative, lauding IRI and CMD’s efforts to champion inclusivity and calling for the continued engagement of political parties to strengthen democratic processes in Kenya. The Commission was presented by Director Legal Services Chrispine Owiye and Manager Partnership Joyce Ekuam.

title: Stakeholders push for early legal reforms to guide IEBC conduct credible General Election17th Feb 2025
text: Stakeholders are calling for timely reforms of electoral related laws to enable the Commission make adequate preparations to guide the conduct of free, fair and credible General Election. Electoral stakeholders said this during the National Conference on Finalizing of Electoral Reforms ahead of the 2027 General Election held from 17th-18th September, 2024 in Nairobi. The participants underscored the need to have an efficient electoral legal framework, independent electoral management body and political good to conduct credible, free and fair elections in Kenya. The two-day conference, organized by the Electoral Law and Governance Institute for Africa (ELGIA), brought together relevant stakeholders to discuss and finalize reforms and related matters ahead of the 2027 General Election. Commission Secretary and CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS noted that the Commission finalized a majority of the proposals and made suggestions for amendments to the election related laws. Further, the Commission has generated amendments to the attendant electoral regulations, which will be subjected to stakeholder engagements and public participation in due course. “The Commission has, over time, made deliberate efforts to put in place a robust electoral-legal framework for the conduct of elections by generating and reviewing legislation and submitting the same to Parliament for consideration. Unfortunately, these amendments are enacted late or too close to the General Election. In certain instances, the proposed laws stall and are not enacted,” noted Marjan. Marjan acknowledged the support different stakeholders have extended to IEBC to strengthen the legal framework including Office of the Attorney General, Office of the Registrar of Political Parties and the Kenya Law Reform Commission. Marjan said he is convinced that the deliberations from the conference will unlock the existing challenges. “We are presented with a momentous opportunity to enact into law all the proposals to enable our country to attain a robust constitutional and legal framework for conduct of free, fair and regular elections based on universal right to vote,” he said.

title: IEBC Media Orientation team visits and engages media firms, learns latest tech operation trends17th Feb 2025
text: The Commission’s Media Orientation and Tour Team visited and engaged seven media organisations with the objective to understand the technological change in their operations and specifically receive feedback on the conduct of the 2022 General Election. The team, which was appointed by Commission Secretary/CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, draws its membership from all nine directorates plus the County Elections Manager, Nairobi, who represents the field offices. Out of these visits, the Commission targets to build trust, enhance media relations, strengthen strategic communications, understand the changing media landscape and receive feedback to inform its policy on how to engage media progressively. The seven media outlets visited included Kenya Broadcasting Corporation (KBC), Royal Media Services (RMS) who runs Citizen Radio and TV, Cape Media Ltd (TV47), Nation Media Group (NMG), Radio Africa Group (Star Newspaper and Radio Jambo), Mediamax Network Ltd (K24 and People Daily) and Signs Media Kenya Ltd. The team also engaged representatives from the Foreign Press Association- Africa (FPAA), which was attended by the CEO. “The Team will undertake courtesy calls as well as orientation visits to various media outlets to enhance media relations and strategic communications, understand the changing media landscape and specifically get feedback with regards to the August 2022, General Election,” Marjan said in the appointment of the Team. The appointment was informed by the recommendations from the Post Election Evaluation report of the 2022 General Election, which sought for continuous media engagement to align the Commission operation with new trends in the industry. In the run up to the 2022 GE, the Commission, together with the Kenya Editors’ Guild (KEG) and Kenya Union of Journalists (KUJ), formed the Kenya Media Sector Working Group (KMSWG) to discuss the challenges, experiences and expectations that would enhance access to electoral information and accurate reporting. Through the KMSWG, over 400 journalists were trained on electoral procedures, which played a crucial role in preparing the media for factual election coverage. Additionally, a media centre was established at the National Tallying Centre by the Commission to enable on-location reporting and provide journalists and media outlets with a live media link on election day. Building on these achievements, in preparation for the 2027 General Election, and considering the changing technology used in the media landscape, the Commission is engaging the media early to gather feedback on the what worked and what did not work, lessons learnt and areas of improvement. The engagements were fruitful with various areas of mutual collaboration raised on how to enhance working relationship to ensure Kenyans get accurate information on the election process. One key area agreed upon was training on media etiquette for Commission staff and training of journalists on the electoral process. The media houses committed to provide a platform for the Commission to tell its own story through various media products such as TV and Radio programs. The team is in the process of compiling a report to be presented to management, which will form the policy that will guide media engagement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

title: Commission submits to Parliamentary Accounts Committee on queries raised by Auditor General17th Feb 2025
text: On Monday 26th August, 2024, the Commission led by Chief Executive Officer Marjan Hussein Marjan submitted to the Parliamentary Accounts Committee (PAC) on various audit queries raised by the Office of the Auditor General. PAC had invited the Commission to shed light on some of the audit queries touching on various sections of the examination Report of the Auditor General on Accounts of National Government for the Financial Year Ended 30th June 2022. The PAC led by Butere Constituency legislator Tindi Mwale afforded the Commission an opportunity to respond to the matters raised in the report. The Committee wanted IEBC to respond to why it has not recovered money owed to it by debtors resulting from court awards. The CEO tabled a response saying it was to engage the services of registered auctioneers to recover the money owed. The Commission also clarified on the number of kits that had been alleged as ‘lost’ by the auditor’s report. The CEO clarified that the report referred to by the Auditor General was an internal document prepared to determine the status of the usability of the KIEMS kits as well as those that had become obsolete. The Committee granted the Commission one month to Liaise with the the Office of the Auditor General to ascertain the accurate count of the number of KIEMS kits owned by the Commission. The CEO was accompanied by the Deputy Commission Secretary Operations Ruth Kulundu, Directors and managers.

title: IEBC joins International Commission of Jurists to validate 2022 election compendium23rd Aug 2024
text: The Commission took part in a validation forum hosted by the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) in Nairobi on 9th August, 2024 that discussed the 2022 Election Compendium. Ruth Makuthu, the Ag. Manager Legal Reforms, Political Parties and Campaign Financing and also a member of ICJ represented the Commission, which was invited owing to its mandate to conduct elections. The Commissions provided insights on how to enhance quality of information compiled that is critical in the validation process to finalize the 2022 Election Compendium. ICJ Kenya, in partnership with Uraia Trust through the support of DANIDA, has been implementing the Electoral Accountability Project that advocates for accountability in the electoral process through engagement with stakeholders. The first phase involved debriefing judges, judicial officers, and lawyers handling election cases, with a focus on Electoral Dispute Resolution (EDR) processes. The second phase involves publishing the Fourth Edition of the Elections Compendium, a vital reference guide for practitioners in the bench, bar, academia, media, and civil society. The compendium reflects the evolving electoral landscape in Kenya and the region, highlighting changes in electoral laws through legislative amendments and judicial pronouncements and it also addresses any gaps.

title: IEBC conducts Little Angels Junior school students election in Malindi Constituency23rd Aug 2024
text: The Commission’s Malindi Constituency Office conducted the Malindi Little Angels Junior School Students Council Elections on 19th June, 2024. The school, which is located in Shella Ward, one of the five wards in the constituency had reached out to the Commission to oversee the conduct of its students’ poll, which the IEBC Malindi Constituency Office agreed to. Little Angels is a day mixed private school with a total population of 543 pupils - 276 Girls and 267 Boys. The elections were for grade four (grade 4) to grade eight (grade 8) classes. Malindi Constituency Assistant Elections Officer Moureen Taabu, who served as the Returning Officer, conducted a series of meetings with the School Elections Committee in the build up to the elections to plan on what materials and personnel are needed.
